# Hashi Documentation for LLMs

> Design specification for Hashi, the Sui native Bitcoin orchestrator.
> Hashi secures and manages BTC for use on Sui through threshold cryptography,
> minting `hBTC` against committee-approved Bitcoin deposits.


- [Introduction](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/index.md): Overview of Hashi, the Sui native Bitcoin orchestrator that secures BTC for use on Sui through threshold cryptography and represents it as hBTC.

## Protocol

- [Service](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/service.md): The Hashi node service that committee members run, the gRPC interface it exposes, and the on-Sui state it relies on.
- [Committee](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/committee.md): The Hashi committee is a subset of the Sui validator set that operates the protocol's MPC signing service.
- [MPC Protocol](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/mpc-protocol.md): The Multi-Party Computation protocols that Hashi uses for distributed key generation, key rotation, and threshold Schnorr signing.
- [Guardian](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/guardian.md): The withdrawal Guardian is a second signatory on managed Bitcoin deposits, providing defense in depth against committee compromise.
- [Bitcoin Address Scheme](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/address-scheme.md): Hashi derives a unique Bitcoin Taproot deposit address for every Sui address using a 2-of-2 multisig between the MPC committee and the Guardian, plus a delayed MPC-only recovery path.
- [Move Model Lifecycle](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/move-model-lifecycle.md): How Hashi's key Move data structures transform between onchain Sui state and offchain Bitcoin state during deposit and withdrawal flows.
- [Deposit](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/deposit.md): How Hashi turns BTC sent to a deposit address into hBTC on Sui through the request, approve, confirm, and mint phases.
- [Withdraw](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/withdraw.md): How Hashi turns hBTC on Sui back into native BTC through the request, approve, build, sign, and broadcast phases.
- [Reconfiguration](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/reconfiguration.md): How the Hashi committee transfers MPC key shares between epochs through DKG or key rotation as Sui validators change.
- [Governance Actions](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/governance-actions.md): Proposal types that the Hashi committee uses to upgrade packages, enable or disable versions, and update onchain configuration.
- [Move Package Upgrades](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/move-upgrades.md): How Hashi classifies Move upgrades as exclusive or non-exclusive, rolls out validator binaries, and retires old package versions safely.
- [Rate Limiting Withdrawals](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/limiter.md): Hashi enforces a token-bucket rate limit on withdrawal outflows through the Guardian to protect against vulnerabilities.
- [Handling Sanctioned Addresses](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/sanctions.md): How Hashi committee members independently apply sanctions checks to deposits and withdrawals with their own TRM Labs accounts.
- [Fees](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/fees.md): How Hashi charges miner fees on withdrawals, enforces fee bounds, and handles stuck transactions.

## hBTC

- [User Flows](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/user-flows.md): End-to-end deposit and withdrawal flows for users moving BTC between Bitcoin and Sui through Hashi.
- [Deposit BTC](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/hbtc/deposit.md): How to deposit BTC into Hashi and receive hBTC on Sui using the Hashi CLI or the TypeScript SDK, from deriving your deposit address to tracking the mint.
- [Withdraw BTC](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/hbtc/withdraw.md): How to redeem hBTC on Sui for native BTC using the Hashi CLI or the TypeScript SDK, including destination address rules, the miner fee, and how to track the withdrawal.
- [Cancel a Withdrawal](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/hbtc/cancel.md): When you can cancel a pending Hashi withdrawal and how to do it with the CLI or the TypeScript SDK to get your hBTC back.
- [hBTC FAQ](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/hbtc/faq.md): Answers to common questions about hBTC: backing, timing, minimums, fees, stuck withdrawals, supported addresses, and the HASHI token.

## Integration

- [TypeScript SDK](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/ts-sdk.md): TypeScript SDK for the Hashi protocol. Hashi is a decentralized Bitcoin collateralization primitive on Sui. Orchestrate native BTC directly from smart contracts—without centralized balance sheets.

## Validators

- [Run a Hashi Node](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/index.md): How Sui validators join the Hashi committee and run a Hashi node, with the onboarding steps, common questions, and links to each operator guide.
- [Prerequisites](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/prerequisites.md): Hardware sizing, the Bitcoin and Sui dependencies, and how to build the Hashi binary before you run a Hashi node.
- [Keys and Security](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/keys.md): The keys a Hashi node uses, which ones you generate, why the validator account key must sign registration, and how to delegate to and revoke an operator key.
- [Configuration](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/configuration.md): The Hashi validator config and CLI config templates for Mainnet and Testnet, the environment variables that override them, and the network ports and TLS the node uses.
- [Genesis and Joining the Committee](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/genesis.md): The Hashi genesis procedure from package publication through registration, launch, and DKG, and how a validator joins the committee after launch.
- [Governance Participation](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/governance.md): How Hashi committee members create, vote on, and execute governance proposals, the proposal types and thresholds, and the configurable protocol parameters.
- [Monitoring and Alerts](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/monitoring.md): The Hashi node Prometheus endpoint, the required metrics push to Mysten, the key metrics to watch, and suggested alerts.
- [Epoch Changes](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/epoch-changes.md): What happens to a Hashi node at each Sui epoch change, what operators must do, and how to recover a stuck reconfiguration.
- [Backup and Restore](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/backup-restore.md): What a Hashi node backup contains, how the node writes one every epoch, and how to restore a node from a backup after machine or disk loss.
- [Hashi Node Backups](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/node-backup.md): How node operators encrypt and restore essential node data with armored PGP backups, including YubiKey restore paths.
- [Troubleshooting](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/validators/troubleshooting.md): Symptoms, causes, and fixes for Hashi node startup failures, CLI configuration errors, registration and offline signing problems, and Bitcoin light client issues.

## Reference

- [Networks](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/reference/networks.md): Hashi Testnet and Mainnet parameters: Sui and Bitcoin chain IDs, package and object IDs, endpoints, ports, and release tags.
- [Configuration](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/config.md): Onchain configuration parameters that control Hashi's deposit, withdrawal, fee, and operational behavior.

- [Releases](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/reference/releases.md): Where to find Hashi releases, how to verify the binary and container image, and how Mysten rolls its Testnet nodes.

## Introduction

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/index.md

> Overview of Hashi, the Sui native Bitcoin orchestrator that secures BTC for use on Sui through threshold cryptography and represents it as hBTC.

Hashi is the Sui native Bitcoin orchestrator. It secures native BTC for use
on Sui and represents that BTC onchain as `hBTC`. This documentation is the
canonical description of Hashi's design, how it operates, and how to
use, integrate, and run it.

## What is Hashi?

Hashi is a protocol that lets you move BTC onto Sui and back without handing
your coins to a single custodian. A committee drawn from the Sui validator
set holds the BTC in a shared pool and signs Bitcoin transactions together
using a threshold Multi-Party Computation (MPC) protocol. No single member
holds the signing key, and the key moves to each new committee as the Sui
validator set changes.

A second, independent signer called the Guardian co-signs every withdrawal
from inside a cloud enclave. Every deposit address requires both the committee
and the Guardian to spend it, so a compromised committee cannot move funds on
its own. See [Guardian](guardian.mdx) and
[Bitcoin Address Scheme](address-scheme.mdx) for the details.

## How does Hashi manage Bitcoin on Sui?

Hashi supports 2 flows, deposit and withdraw:

- **Deposit:** Every Sui address has its own unique Bitcoin deposit address.
  You send BTC to yours, then tell Hashi about the transaction on Sui. After
  the committee confirms the deposit on Bitcoin, Hashi mints an equal amount
  of `hBTC` to your Sui address.
- **Withdraw:** You submit `hBTC` and a destination Bitcoin address on Sui.
  Hashi burns the `hBTC`, builds a Bitcoin transaction from its pool, signs it
  with the committee and the Guardian, and broadcasts it.

Deposits are free and withdrawals pay only the Bitcoin miner fee. There is no
protocol fee. See [User Flows](user-flows.mdx) for the end-to-end picture and
[Fees](fees.mdx) for the numbers.

## What is hBTC?

`hBTC` is a fungible `Coin<BTC>` on Sui that Hashi mints on deposit and burns
on withdrawal. Each `hBTC` corresponds to BTC that the committee and Guardian
hold in the Hashi pool. Because `hBTC` is a standard Sui coin, you can use it
in any Sui app, for example as collateral in a lending protocol.

:::info

`hBTC` is the only coin Hashi creates. There is no HASHI governance, utility,
or airdrop token. Committee members govern the protocol by voting onchain with
their validator stake weight. Treat any HASHI token offering, presale, or
airdrop as an imitation.

:::

## Where do I start?

The documentation has 5 sections. Choose the one that matches what you want
to do:

- **hBTC:** Move BTC in and out. Start with [User Flows](user-flows.mdx),
  then follow [Deposit BTC](hbtc/deposit.mdx),
  [Withdraw BTC](hbtc/withdraw.mdx), and
  [Cancel a Withdrawal](hbtc/cancel.mdx), and check the
  [hBTC FAQ](hbtc/faq.mdx).
- **Protocol:** How Hashi works. Start with the architecture pages, then
  read the [Deposit](deposit.mdx) and [Withdraw](withdraw.mdx) lifecycles, [Reconfiguration](reconfiguration.mdx),
  governance, security, and [Fees](fees.mdx).
- **Integration:** Build on Hashi with the [TypeScript SDK](ts-sdk.mdx).
- **Validators:** Join the committee and run a node. Start with the
  [Run a Hashi Node](validators/index.mdx) and keep
  [Hashi Node Backups](node-backup.mdx) nearby.
- **Reference:** Onchain [configuration parameters](config.mdx), plus the
  Move package, the gRPC API, and the Rust API.

---

## Service

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/service.md

> The Hashi node service that committee members run, the gRPC interface it exposes, and the on-Sui state it relies on.

Every committee member is responsible for running a Hashi node service. Each
Hashi node exposes an HTTP service, secured by Transport Layer Security (TLS)
using a self-signed cert (each member registers its ed25519 public key in the
`CommitteeSet` on the `Hashi` object), and serves the gRPC `BridgeService` and
`MpcService`. Peers connect with their own registered TLS key, and the node
refuses any caller whose key belongs to no registered validator, except on
`/health` and `/ready`.

## How should liveness probes check the node?

The node runs 2 HTTP listeners: the TLS-secured service described above, and
a separate plain-HTTP metrics listener. The `/health` on the TLS service always
answers; liveness probes should use the `/health` on the plain-HTTP metrics
listener instead, which fails once the node's main runtime stops running tasks
for 2 minutes.

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `metrics-http-address` | `127.0.0.1:9180` | Address of the plain-HTTP metrics listener, whose `/health` liveness probes should use. |

## How is the Hashi Move package published?

- Hashi publishes its Move package as a normal package. It is not a system
  package and is not part of the Sui framework.

## Is the Hashi service stateless?

A main goal of this design is to make the Hashi service as stateless as
possible. Outside of any cryptographic material required for participating in
the protocol, any state critical for the functioning of the service must be
stored on Sui as part of the live object set. Correct operation of the
service must not depend on knowledge of historical transactions or events
previously emitted.

The set of data structures and state kept onchain is as follows:

```mermaid
block-beta
  columns 1

  block
    committee
    config
  end

  pool["UTXO pool"]

  block
    gov["Governance Requests"]
    deposits["Deposit Request Queue"]
    withdrawals["Withdrawal Request Queue"]
  end

  broadcast["Ordered broadcast channel"]
```

---

## Committee

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/committee.md

> The Hashi committee is a subset of the Sui validator set that operates the protocol's MPC signing service.

Hashi is a native protocol, meaning the members of the Hashi committee are a
subset of the Sui validators. Only members of the Sui validator set can join
the Hashi committee, but membership is otherwise optional, because it
requires a separate onchain registration and running extra services. In
practice, Mysten Labs expects more than 90% of Sui validators to join the
Hashi committee.

## Registration information

Each Sui validator must register before joining the Hashi committee. Each
committee member provides the following additional information:

```rust
struct HashiNodeInfo {
    /// Sui Validator Address of this node
    validator_address: address,

    /// Sui Address of an operations account 
    operator_address: address,

    /// bls12381 public key to be used in the next epoch.
    ///
    /// This public key can be rotated but will only take effect at the
    /// beginning of the next epoch.
    next_epoch_public_key: Element<UncompressedG1>,

    /// The publicly reachable URL where the `hashi` service for this validator
    /// can be reached.
    ///
    /// This URL can be rotated and any such updates will take effect
    /// immediately.
    endpoint_url: String,

    /// ed25519 public key used to verify TLS self-signed x509 certs
    ///
    /// This public key can be rotated and any such updates will take effect
    /// immediately.
    tls_public_key: vector<u8>,
}
```

The voting weight each validator possesses mirrors the
`SuiSystemState`. This is the stake weight behind the `2f+1` participation
requirement described in [Committee hand-offs](#committee-hand-offs).

## Why the committee is not exactly the set of Sui validators

The Hashi committee is a subset of the Sui validators rather than strictly the
same set. There are a few challenges with forcing these sets to be identical:

- Membership in the committee is strictly optional, because Hashi's system
  state is separate from Sui's system state. When someone registers as a Sui
  validator, the required metadata (public keys, network addresses, and so on)
  only includes information necessary for running the `sui-node` validator
  service. Without changes, there is no way to require a new Sui validator to
  also register for the Hashi committee.
- Enforcing tight coupling would require changes to Sui's epoch change and
  reconfiguration process in a few ways:
  - The MPC hand-off protocol takes a non-trivial amount of time to execute,
    so Sui would need to lock in the new set of validators some time period
    before the close of the epoch, giving the MPC committee time to
    reconfigure.
  - Sui's epoch change and reconfiguration would need to block on successful
    reconfiguration of the MPC committee.

Addressing any of the above would require deep changes to Sui's
reconfiguration process. Some of those changes are directly opposed by the
core team, and any of them would take significant time to implement correctly.

## Committee hand-offs

The one downside of not having tight coupling is the need to handle the
hand-off from an old committee to a new committee. At each epoch boundary after
genesis, the key rotation protocol transfers key shares from the old committee
to the new one. At genesis, no old committee exists to hand off from, so the
first committee runs distributed key generation (DKG) instead. The hand-off
requires that
`2f+1` stake-weighted members of the old committee are alive and willing to
participate in the hand-off protocol. This design makes that assumption,
because of the challenges of enforcing tight coupling, and a later version
can add an economic mechanism to motivate older committee members to
participate in the hand-off process.

---

## MPC Protocol

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/mpc-protocol.md

> The Multi-Party Computation protocols that Hashi uses for distributed key generation, key rotation, and threshold Schnorr signing.

> For a comprehensive technical analysis and formal security proofs, see the [Hashi MPC Whitepaper](./Hashi_MPC_Whitepaper_v1.pdf).

## What MPC protocols does Hashi use?

Sui validators use several Multi-Party Computation (MPC) protocols to
implement a threshold Schnorr signer: Distributed Key Generation (DKG) for
generating a key, key rotation for redistributing the key on committee
changes, and a distributed signing protocol for signing transactions. The
Mysten Labs cryptography team based the protocols on prior published work and
modified and improved them.

## What are the liveness and security parameters for Hashi MPC?

Two values, `f` and `t`, parametrize these protocols, such that Hashi
operates as long as fewer than `f` of the staking power is unresponsive
(liveness), and is secure as long as fewer than `t` of the staking power
is colluding. In the first version of Hashi, the team expects `t` to be in the
range of 33% to 50%, and `f` in the range of 20% to 33%. These values
might increase in future versions of Hashi.

| Parameter | Property | Hashi has this property while | Expected range in the first version |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `f` | Liveness | fewer than `f` of the staking power is unresponsive | 20% to 33% |
| `t` | Security | fewer than `t` of the staking power is colluding | 33% to 50% |

## Why does Hashi use a second signer?

In addition to the MPC signer, Hashi uses a second signer implemented with a
cloud enclave that enforces policies independently of the MPC protocols,
reducing the risk of collusion or supply-chain attacks.

---

## Guardian

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/guardian.md

> The withdrawal Guardian is a second signatory on managed Bitcoin deposits, providing defense in depth against committee compromise.

To protect against vulnerabilities and against malicious past committees,
Hashi uses a withdrawal guardian: a second signatory on the managed Bitcoin
deposits. Spending a deposit requires a 2-of-2 multisig where the guardian is one
party and the Hashi MPC committee is the other. A recovery script also lets the
MPC committee alone spend a UTXO 60 days after it confirms (see
[Bitcoin Address Scheme](address-scheme.mdx)).

## Components

The guardian integration has five distinct flows:

- **Ceremony mode** is the key-generation control-plane flow. The operator
  initializes a ceremony guardian, supplies the key provisioner (KP) roster,
  and receives the guardian BTC public key plus encrypted KP shares.
- **Withdraw-mode provisioning** arms a standby withdrawal guardian while the
  current active guardian is still alive. The operator installs a stable
  `InitConfig`; each KP independently recomputes `config_hash` from its locally
  configured limiter config and deployment config (S3 bucket and region,
  retention environment, network, and PCR allowlist), requires it to match the
  enclave's, and submits threshold encrypted shares through the public relay.
  Because the hash covers both the limiter config and the deployment config, a
  KP releases its share only to an enclave running the configuration that KP
  expects.
- **Activation** is the operator-triggered takeover step. The standby enclave
  confirms a quiet window, derives live state from S3, checks the operator's
  expected state hash, records activation, and only then serves withdrawals.
- **Normal operation** is a data-plane flow. MPC nodes call the guardian proxy's
  node endpoint for guardian info, withdrawal signatures, and committee handoff
  updates.
- **KP rotation** re-deals the guardian key to a new KP set on a fresh ceremony
  guardian (`RotateKpSet`, then every new KP confirms), or replaces one KP's
  certificate (`ProvisionerRotateCert`).

The main components are:

- **MPC nodes**: the Hashi validator committee. Nodes collect committee
  certificates, run the MPC signer, and call the guardian for the second
  Bitcoin signature.
- **Guardian proxy**: the guardian's gRPC endpoints. The public one
  (`guardian_url`) serves `/info`, `GetGuardianInfo`, the attested info
  queries, and the key-provisioner RPCs (the share relay, `ConfirmCeremony`,
  and `ProvisionerRotateCert`); it never serves operator RPCs, which reach the
  enclave directly. Nodes call a separate one (`guardian_node_url`), which serves only
  `GetGuardianInfo` and node RPCs: the proxy terminates TLS itself and forwards
  node RPCs only for current or pending committee members, who present their
  registered TLS key as a client certificate. It forwards a committee handoff
  only once the chain stores it, which happens when its reconfiguration
  completes, so no node can move the guardian to a committee whose
  reconfiguration is later aborted. Both checks trust the proxy's Sui fullnode
  for chain state, and assume nodes cannot reach the enclave directly.
- **Guardian enclave**: the private signer and policy engine. A standby
  guardian stores static config and the reconstructed BTC key; an active
  guardian additionally verifies committee certificates, enforces the limiter,
  and signs Bitcoin inputs. A standby does not serve withdrawals: the operator arms it
  while the current active guardian is still alive and takes over from it only
  after operator-triggered activation. Every session signs the records it
  writes to S3.
- **Key provisioners (KPs)**: independent holders of guardian key shares. Each
  share has one configured YubiKey-backed OpenPGP certificate and one encrypted
  ciphertext.
- **Operator**: the off-enclave actor that drives guardian ceremony and
  withdraw-mode provisioning and activation.
- **S3**: signed log storage under Object Lock for init (attestation and
  session lifecycle), heartbeat, ceremony proposal, ceremony, KP-share,
  genesis, withdrawal, and committee-update records. Heartbeats, ceremony
  proposals, and KP shares get only a short lock. Activation records are
  session lifecycle records in the activating session's init log.
- **Onchain Hashi state**: the source of committee, config, withdrawal, and MPC
  key state used by nodes and initialization tooling.

## Ceremony mode flow

Before the ceremony, each KP provides its public OpenPGP certificate, fingerprint
text file, and three matching PEM sidecars. See the
[KP provisioning guide](https://github.com/MystenLabs/hashi/blob/main/key-provisioner/provision.md#setting-up-your-yubikey)
for device requirements, output filenames, and attestation policy.

Configuration still contains only `.asc` paths. All matching sidecars must be
colocated on every certificate-loading host, including for signers and replacement
certificates. The CLI verifies and sends bundles; the guardian independently
rejects missing or invalid proofs on every certificate-bearing RPC.
The sole usable signing key must be the SIG-attested primary key, so the KP's
primary-key fingerprint identifies its attested signing key. The guardian rejects certificates with
a separate signing subkey under an unattested primary.
Signature verification pins that signing key; encryption and recipient checks
pin the attested DEC key. Each share ciphertext must contain exactly one
OpenPGP recipient matching that DEC key.
YubiKey provenance checks are separate from the guardian's Nitro attestation
in its S3 init log.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber

    participant Operator
    participant S3
    participant Guardian as Guardian enclave
    participant KPs as Key provisioners

    Operator->>Guardian: OperatorInit(deployment config, S3 credentials)
    Guardian->>S3: log(init attestation + GuardianInfo)
    Operator->>Guardian: SetupNewKey(KP attested bundles, n, t)
    Guardian->>Guardian: Verify all YubiKey proofs, bind SIG/DEC keys, and assign share ids in fingerprint order
    Guardian->>S3: log(kp-shares/proposed/{session})
    Guardian-->>Operator: encrypted KP share state + guardian BTC pubkey

    KPs->>S3: Read init and the session's proposed ceremony
    S3-->>KPs: One PGP-encrypted share targeting this KP's attested DEC key
    KPs->>KPs: Decrypt share and verify Nitro attestation, recipients, commitment
    KPs->>Guardian: Confirm proposed ceremony digest
    Guardian->>S3: Once all n KPs confirm, publish kp-shares state, then ceremony commit
```

## Guardian info queries

`GetGuardianInfo` returns the guardian's self-reported state, with no
signature or attestation. The proxy caches these responses for 30 seconds and
drops the cache after each signed withdrawal; the public HTTP `/info` view
keeps its own cache (`INFO_CACHE_TTL_MS`, 30 seconds by default).

KPs and operators use `GetAttestedGuardianInfo` to receive signed guardian state
alongside a fresh Nitro attestation. Attested responses are never cached.
`GetProvisioningTargetInfo` forwards to that RPC on the provisioning guardian
(the standby when configured, otherwise the active guardian), also without caching.

The distinct RPC paths allow deployments to restrict attestation queries while
leaving ordinary info public. The proxy does not itself add authentication for
these queries: an access policy must cover both `GetAttestedGuardianInfo` and
`GetProvisioningTargetInfo`.

Clients that previously set `include_attestation` on `GetGuardianInfo` must switch
to `GetAttestedGuardianInfo`. Ordinary info no longer returns an attestation or a signature. Upgrade the guardian and proxy before
switching KP and operator clients to the new RPC.

## Withdraw-mode provisioning flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber

    participant Operator
    participant S3
    participant Guardian as Standby guardian enclave
    participant Proxy as Guardian proxy
    participant KPs as Key provisioners

    Note over Operator,Guardian: Operator initialization
    Operator->>Operator: Gather limiter config plus deployment config (bucket, region, retention environment, network, PCR allowlist)
    Operator->>Operator: Build InitConfig
    Operator->>Operator: Require S3 state to match --do-genesis intent
    Operator->>Operator: With flag, build GenesisState from committee plus Hashi object id plus master G
    Operator->>Guardian: OperatorInit(S3 credentials, InitConfig, optional GenesisState)
    Guardian->>S3: Read latest ceremony and KP-share state, plus genesis record on later deploys
    Guardian->>Guardian: Snapshot CeremonyState for this arming
    Guardian->>S3: log(init GuardianInfo(config_hash, optional genesis_state_hash, sharing instance))
    Guardian->>S3: start heartbeat stream from OI onward

    Note over KPs,Guardian: Threshold share provisioning
    KPs->>Proxy: GetProvisioningTargetInfo
    Proxy->>Guardian: GetAttestedGuardianInfo
    Proxy-->>KPs: config_hash plus optional genesis_state_hash plus session_id plus n/t plus attestation
    KPs->>KPs: Require S3 state to match --do-genesis intent
    KPs->>KPs: Verify PCRs and derive config hash plus optional genesis-state hash
    KPs->>S3: Read latest ceremony and kp-shares state
    KPs->>KPs: Decrypt own share and check its commitment
    KPs->>KPs: HPKE-encrypt the share to guardian session key (no AAD)
    KPs->>KPs: Sign(session_id, config_hash, optional genesis_state_hash, encrypted share)
    KPs->>Proxy: SingleProvisionerInit(signed submission)
    Proxy->>Proxy: Pre-verify KP signature and relay roster
    Proxy->>Guardian: Fetch live session, config/genesis hashes, and provisioning status
    Guardian-->>Proxy: session_id, config_hash, optional genesis_state_hash, n/t, provisioned flag
    alt fewer than threshold shares collected
        Proxy-->>KPs: signed submission accepted, waiting for threshold
    else threshold reached
        Proxy->>Guardian: ProvisionerInit(T signed submissions)
        Guardian->>Guardian: Verify signatures, session/config/genesis pins, and KP assignments
        Guardian->>Guardian: Decrypt without AAD and verify commitments
        Guardian->>Guardian: Reconstruct BTC key and mark armed standby
        opt first deploy
            Guardian->>S3: log(genesis committee, Hashi object id, and master G)
        end
        Guardian->>S3: log(init fully-initialized)
        Proxy-->>KPs: standby armed
    end
```

On first deploy, the operator and every KP pass `--do-genesis`. This is purely an
explicit intent marker: callers fail if it disagrees with the observed S3
committee state. The operator pins the current onchain committee, configured
Hashi object id, and MPC master `G` as an optional `GenesisState` during
`OperatorInit`, and each KP independently derives its hash and includes it in
the normal signed PI submission. Once PI reaches threshold, the enclave writes
the committee, Hashi object id, and master `G` to `genesis/record.json`. Later
deploys use `None` and do not pass the flag; their enclave loads the Hashi
object id and master `G` from `genesis/record.json` instead.

## Standby activation flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber

    participant Operator
    participant S3
    participant Guardian as Guardian enclave

    Operator->>Guardian: Read pinned ceremony instance from GuardianInfo
    Operator->>S3: Download committee/genesis plus limiter post-state
    Operator->>Operator: Compute expected_state_hash
    Operator->>Guardian: OperatorActivate(expected_state_hash)

    Guardian->>S3: Confirm all other sessions heartbeat-quiet for QUIET_PERIOD
    Guardian->>S3: Read latest committee-update or genesis record
    Guardian->>S3: Recover limiter state from max-seq success or genesis
    Guardian->>Guardian: Derive ActivationState and state_hash
    Guardian->>Guardian: Refuse if derived hash differs from operator pin
    Guardian->>S3: log(init operator-activation record)
    Guardian->>Guardian: Install derived state and mark active
```

## Normal operation flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber

    participant Onchain as Onchain Hashi state
    participant MPC as MPC nodes
    participant Proxy as Guardian proxy
    participant Guardian as Active guardian enclave
    participant S3
    participant Bitcoin

    Note over MPC,Guardian: Guardian info
    MPC->>Guardian: GetGuardianInfo via proxy
    Guardian-->>MPC: GuardianInfo

    Note over Onchain,Guardian: Withdrawal signing
    MPC->>Onchain: Read pending withdrawal transaction
    MPC->>MPC: Produce MPC signatures for each Bitcoin input
    MPC->>Onchain: Store MPC signatures
    MPC->>Proxy: StandardWithdrawal(cert, wid, utxos, seq, timestamp)
    Proxy->>Proxy: Replay stored signatures for an already-signed wid (memory or S3 withdraw log)
    Proxy->>Guardian: Forward a wid with no withdraw record
    Guardian->>Guardian: Require active session then verify cert then consume limiter tokens then sign BTC inputs
    Guardian->>S3: log(withdraw success)
    Guardian-->>MPC: Guardian BTC signatures via proxy
    MPC->>Onchain: Finalize withdrawal with Guardian signatures
    MPC->>Bitcoin: Broadcast fully signed transaction

    Note over Onchain,Guardian: Committee handoff catch-up
    MPC->>Onchain: Read stored committee handoffs
    MPC->>MPC: Chain the stored handoffs from the guardian's epoch to the current one
    MPC->>Proxy: UpdateCommitteeChain(signed handoffs)
    Proxy->>Onchain: Check that each handoff is stored
    Proxy->>Guardian: Forward the stored handoffs
    Guardian->>S3: log(committee-update)
    Guardian-->>MPC: current_committee_epoch via proxy
```

---

## Bitcoin Address Scheme

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/address-scheme.md

> Hashi derives a unique Bitcoin Taproot deposit address for every Sui address using a 2-of-2 multisig between the MPC committee and the Guardian, plus a delayed MPC-only recovery path.

Every Sui address has its own unique Hashi Bitcoin deposit address. This gives
Hashi a lightweight way to identify which Sui address to credit for a deposit.
All Hashi deposit addresses are `P2TR` (Pay-to-Taproot) with a Taproot tree of
two leaves:

1. A 2-of-2 multisig script between Hashi and the Guardian, used for all
   normal spends.
2. A recovery script that lets the Hashi key alone spend the output after a
   60-day BIP-68 relative timelock enforced by `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY`
   (BIP-112). This is an
   escape hatch: if the Guardian key is ever lost, funds become recoverable by
   the MPC committee once the delay elapses. The delay counts from when
   the UTXO confirms, and the script encodes it, so changing it changes
   every deposit address.

## What is the exact descriptor?

The exact [descriptor](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/descriptors.md)
is:

```
tr({i}, {multi_a(2, {g}, {h}), and_v(v:older({delay}), pk({h}))})
```

where:

- `H` is the base Hashi MPC public key, available onchain.
- `h = derive(H, d)` is the child public key derived from `H` using
  derivation path `d` (the depositor's Sui address).
- `g` is the guardian's fixed public key.
- `delay` is the 60-day relative timelock, encoded as the BIP-68 sequence
  `0x0040278D` (`4_204_429`).
  [How is the 60-day delay encoded?](#how-is-the-60-day-delay-encoded) breaks
  down the encoding step by step.
- `i` is the NUMS (nothing-up-my-sleeve) internal key defined in BIP-341
  (`50929b74c1a04954b78b4b6035e97a5e078a5a0f28ec96d547bfee9ace803ac0`)
  with no known private key, ensuring all spends occur through the script path.

Read left to right, the descriptor says: the Taproot internal key is `i`, and
the tree has 2 script leaves. `multi_a(2, {g}, {h})` is the 2-of-2 multisig
leaf, which needs signatures from both the guardian key `g` and the child MPC
key `h`. `and_v(v:older({delay}), pk({h}))` is the recovery leaf, which needs
the `delay` to have elapsed and a signature from `h` alone.

## How is the 60-day delay encoded?

Use the BIP-68 sequence value `0x0040278D` (`4_204_429`) for `delay`. To build
the value:

1. Express 60 days in seconds: `60 * 24 * 60 * 60` = `5_184_000`.
2. Convert to 512-second units, rounding up:
   `ceil(5_184_000 / 512)` = `10_125`. This is a count of 512-second units in
   60 days, not a count of blocks.
3. OR in the time-based type bit, `1 << 22` (`4_194_304`):
   `4_194_304 | 10_125` = `4_204_429` = `0x0040278D`.

## How is a deposit address derived from a Sui address?

To derive the deposit address for a Sui address:

1. Take the depositor's Sui address as the derivation path `d`.
2. Derive the child public key `h = derive(H, d)` from the base Hashi MPC
   public key `H`, which is available onchain.
3. Substitute `h`, the guardian's public key `g`, the encoded `delay`, and the
   NUMS internal key `i` into the descriptor above.

The resulting P2TR address is the deposit address for that Sui address. Hashi
credits any deposit to it to that Sui address.

The key derivation is not BIP-32. It is a purpose-built unhardened derivation
over secp256k1, keyed by the Sui address, giving each depositor a unique
Bitcoin address while the master signing key remains shared across the MPC
committee.

## How does withdrawal funding treat older deposit UTXOs?

Normal withdrawal funding remains largest-first. Within the existing
fee-eligible consolidation budget, confirmed UTXOs older than 4,320 blocks are
prioritized before ordinary smallest-first candidates. The 4,320-block
threshold estimates 30 days using Bitcoin's ten-minute block target; actual
MPC-only recovery eligibility remains governed by the time-based CSV script
above.

---

## Move Model Lifecycle

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/move-model-lifecycle.md

> How Hashi's key Move data structures transform between onchain Sui state and offchain Bitcoin state during deposit and withdrawal flows.

This document illustrates the lifecycle of key Move models in the deposit and
withdrawal flows, showing how data structures transform between onchain (Sui)
and offchain (Bitcoin) states.

## What is the entry-function gating principle?

Every entry function that takes the `Hashi` object asserts the package
version is enabled. Beyond that, **pause and reconfiguration gate only the
deposit and withdrawal flows.** The table shows which entry functions stop
when governance pauses the system and which stop while a committee handoff is
pending.

| Entry functions | Stops during a pause | Stops while a committee handoff is pending |
| --------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Deposit approval (`approve_deposit()`) and confirmation (`confirm_deposit()`) | Yes | Yes |
| Withdrawal approval (`approve_request()`), commitment, signing, and finalization (`finalize_withdrawal()`) | Yes | Yes |
| User requests (`deposit()`, `request_withdrawal()`) | Yes | No |
| Withdrawal confirmation (`confirm_withdrawal()`) | Yes | No |
| Withdrawal cancellation | No | No |
| Reconfiguration, MPC certificate submission, governance | No | No |
| Cleanup entries: `cleanup_spent_utxos`, `archive_confirmed_withdrawals`, `archive_withdrawal_requests`, `finish_archive_withdrawal_txns`, `destroy_key_gen_certs`, `destroy_nonce_certs`, `delete_expired_deposit`, `proposal::delete_expired` | No | No |
| Validator registration or key rotation | No | No |

The last 4 rows never check pause, because an
emergency pause must not block operators from maintaining nodes or the chain
from shedding dead state. Nodes themselves stop all leader work while paused,
garbage collection included, so during a pause only a
manual call sheds that state. One asymmetry is intentional: users can request deposits and
withdrawals during reconfiguration (a withdrawal request only escrows their
hBTC); only committee approval, commitment, signing, and deposit confirmation
wait for the new committee.

## How do Move models change during a deposit?

During a reconfiguration, users can still call `deposit()`, but approval and
confirmation wait for the new committee; see
[What is the entry-function gating principle?](#what-is-the-entry-function-gating-principle).

```mermaid
---
title: Deposit Flow - Move Model Lifecycle
---
flowchart TD
    subgraph Bitcoin["Bitcoin Network"]
        BTC_UTXO["Bitcoin UTXO<br/>(txid:vout, amount)"]
    end

    subgraph Committee["Hashi Protocol Committee"]
        MEMBERS["Committee Members<br/>(Sui Validators)"]
        SCREEN["AML screening<br/>(members with a TRM API key, mainnet only)"]
        SIGN["Aggregate BLS Signatures"]
        CERT["CommitteeSignature<br/>{ epoch, signature, signers_bitmap }"]
        VERIFY["verify_certificate()<br/>threshold check"]
    end

    subgraph Sui["Sui Chain"]
        subgraph DepositPhase["1. Request Phase"]
            DR["DepositRequest<br/>{ id, sender, created_timestamp_ms,<br/>sui_tx_digest, utxo, approval_cert,<br/>approved_timestamp_ms, confirmed_timestamp_ms }"]
            DRQ["DepositRequestQueue<br/>.requests"]
        end

        subgraph ApprovePhase["2. Approval Phase"]
            APPROVED["DepositRequest (approved)<br/>approval_cert: Some(cert)<br/>approved_timestamp_ms: Some(t)"]
        end

        subgraph ConfirmPhase["3. Confirmation Phase"]
            DELAY["Time-delay window<br/>(bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms)"]
            CERTIFIED["CertifiedMessage&lt;DepositConfirmationMessage&gt;<br/>{ message, signature, stake_support }"]
            UTXO["Utxo<br/>{ id, amount, derivation_path }"]
            POOL["UtxoPool<br/>.utxo_records"]
            MINT["Treasury.mint_balance()"]
            BAL["Balance&lt;BTC&gt;<br/>(sent to the recipient's address balance)"]
        end
    end

    BTC_UTXO -->|"User creates request<br/>with UTXO info"| DR
    DR -->|"deposit()"| DRQ
    DRQ -.->|"Observe request"| MEMBERS
    MEMBERS -->|"Wait for BTC confirmations,<br/>then screen BTC tx & Sui recipient"| SCREEN
    SCREEN -->|"Sign deposit request"| SIGN
    SIGN -->|"Quorum reached"| CERT
    CERT -->|"approve_deposit()"| VERIFY
    VERIFY -->|"Valid certificate"| APPROVED
    APPROVED --> DELAY
    DELAY -->|"confirm_deposit()<br/>(re-verifies cert)"| CERTIFIED
    CERTIFIED --> UTXO
    UTXO -->|"Insert"| POOL
    UTXO -->|"Extract amount"| MINT
    MINT -->|"Mint tokens"| BAL

    style Bitcoin fill:#f7931a,color:#fff
    style Committee fill:#E91E8A,color:#fff
    style Sui fill:#4da2ff,color:#fff
    style BAL fill:#00d4aa,color:#000
    style BTC_UTXO fill:#f7931a,color:#fff
    style CERT fill:#E91E8A,color:#fff
    style CERTIFIED fill:#00d4aa,color:#000
```

### Deposit flow summary

| Step | Actor             | Action                                           | Model Transformation                                                                  |
| ---- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | User              | User sends BTC to bridge address                 | Bitcoin UTXO created                                                                  |
| 2    | User              | User calls `deposit()`                           | `DepositRequest` → `DepositRequestQueue`                                              |
| 3    | Committee members | Committee members wait for Bitcoin confirmations | `bitcoin_confirmation_threshold` blocks on the deposit transaction                    |
| 4    | Committee members | Committee members screen and sign request        | Members with a TRM API key screen it (Mainnet only); BLS signatures aggregated → `CommitteeSignature` |
| 5    | Leader            | Leader calls `approve_deposit()` with cert       | `verify_certificate()` → request stores `approval_cert` and `approved_timestamp_ms`   |
| 6    | None              | Time-delay window elapses                        | `bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms` (a window to catch a faulty approval and pause before the contract mints anything) |
| 7    | Anyone            | Anyone calls `confirm_deposit()`                 | Re-`verify_certificate()` → `CertifiedMessage<DepositConfirmationMessage>`            |
| 8    | Treasury          | Treasury mints tokens                            | If the UTXO has a derivation path, `Utxo.amount` → `Balance<BTC>` sent to that address |
| 9    | None              | Certified request processed                      | `Utxo` → `UtxoPool`; `DepositRequest` → `DepositRequestQueue.processed` with `confirmed_timestamp_ms` set |

---

## How do Move models change during a withdrawal?

During a reconfiguration, users can still call `request_withdrawal()` and
withdrawal confirmation still proceeds, but approval, commitment, signing, and
finalization wait for the new committee; see
[What is the entry-function gating principle?](#what-is-the-entry-function-gating-principle).

```mermaid
---
title: Withdrawal Flow - Move Model Lifecycle
---
flowchart TD
    subgraph Sui["Sui Chain"]
        subgraph RequestPhase["1. Request Phase"]
            BAL["Balance&lt;BTC&gt;<br/>(User's tokens)"]
            WR["WithdrawalRequest<br/>{ id, btc_amount, bitcoin_address }"]
            WRQ["WithdrawalRequestQueue<br/>.requests"]
        end

        subgraph ProcessPhase["2. Processing Phase"]
            UTXO_POOL["UtxoPool<br/>"]
            BURN["Treasury.burn()"]
            PW["WithdrawalTransaction<br/>{ id, txid, request_ids, inputs,<br/>withdrawal_outputs, change_outputs,<br/>signing, guardian_signatures }"]
            PWQ["WithdrawalRequestQueue<br/>.withdrawal_txns"]
        end

        subgraph SignPhase["3. Signature Storage Phase"]
            SUBMIT_SIGS["commit_input_signatures()<br/>Store MPC sigs on-chain in chunks"]
            FINALIZE["finalize_withdrawal()<br/>Attach guardian sigs"]
            PW_SIGNED["WithdrawalTransaction<br/>(with signatures)"]
        end

        subgraph ConfirmPhase["4. Confirmation Phase"]
            CERTIFIED2["CertifiedMessage&lt;WithdrawalConfirmationMessage&gt;"]
            MOVE_CONFIRMED["Set confirmed_timestamp_ms<br/>(GC later moves it to .confirmed_txns)"]
            RECORD["Mark input UTXOs spent<br/>(GC later moves them to spent_utxos)"]
        end
    end

    subgraph Committee["Hashi Protocol Committee"]
        MEMBERS2["Committee Members<br/>(Sui Validators)"]
        SCREEN2["AML screening<br/>(members with a TRM API key, mainnet only)"]
        VOTE["Vote to process withdrawal<br/>& select UTXOs"]
        VAL["validate_consume()<br/>leader's read-only<br/>seq + capacity check"]
        MPC["MPC Signing Protocol"]
        BLS_GW["Aggregate BLS cert over<br/>StandardWithdrawalRequest<br/>(wid, seq, ts, utxos)"]
        LL["LocalLimiter<br/>(per-node cache:<br/>next_seq, tokens)"]
        SIGN2["Aggregate BLS Signatures"]
        CERT2["CommitteeSignature"]
    end

    subgraph Guardian["Hashi Guardian (off-chain rate limiter)"]
        GRL["RateLimiter<br/>{ next_seq,<br/>num_tokens_available, last_updated_at }"]
        STD_RPC["StandardWithdrawal RPC<br/>verifies committee cert,<br/>consumes from limiter,<br/>returns enclave signature"]
    end

    subgraph Bitcoin["Bitcoin Network"]
        BTC_TX["Bitcoin Transaction<br/>(signed via MPC)"]
        BTC_UTXO["Bitcoin UTXO<br/>(at destination)"]
    end

    BAL -->|"User deposits<br/>Balance&lt;BTC&gt;"| WR
    WR -->|"request_withdrawal()"| WRQ
    WRQ -.->|"Observe & approve<br/>request"| MEMBERS2
    MEMBERS2 -->|"Screen BTC destination<br/>& Sui requester"| SCREEN2
    SCREEN2 --> VOTE
    VOTE -.->|"Select UTXOs<br/>(off-chain)"| UTXO_POOL
    VOTE --> BURN
    BURN -->|"Balance&lt;BTC&gt; burned,<br/>WithdrawalTransaction created"| PW
    PW --> PWQ
    PWQ -.->|"Observe withdrawal<br/>transactions"| MPC
    MPC -->|"Schnorr witness signatures<br/>per input"| SUBMIT_SIGS
    SUBMIT_SIGS -.->|"all inputs signed"| VAL
    LL -.->|"current next_seq,<br/>capacity"| VAL
    VAL -->|"validation passes"| BLS_GW
    BLS_GW -->|"finalize_withdrawal_<br/>through_guardian"| STD_RPC
    STD_RPC -->|"consume(seq, ts, amt)"| GRL
    GRL -.->|"GetGuardianInfo<br/>(seed, then periodic reconcile)"| LL
    STD_RPC -->|"guardian signatures"| FINALIZE
    FINALIZE -->|"cert over MPC +<br/>guardian signatures"| PW_SIGNED
    PW_SIGNED -.->|"fully signed (object mirror):<br/>apply_consume(next_seq, ts, amt)"| LL
    PW_SIGNED -->|"Reconstruct & broadcast<br/>signed BTC tx"| BTC_TX
    BTC_TX --> BTC_UTXO
    BTC_UTXO -.->|"Observe confirmation<br/>(N confirmations)"| SIGN2
    SIGN2 --> CERT2
    CERT2 -->|"confirm_withdrawal()"| CERTIFIED2
    CERTIFIED2 --> MOVE_CONFIRMED
    MOVE_CONFIRMED --> RECORD

    style Bitcoin fill:#f7931a,color:#fff
    style Committee fill:#E91E8A,color:#fff
    style Sui fill:#4da2ff,color:#fff
    style Guardian fill:#7B1FA2,color:#fff
    style BAL fill:#00d4aa,color:#000
    style BTC_UTXO fill:#f7931a,color:#fff
    style CERT2 fill:#E91E8A,color:#fff
    style CERTIFIED2 fill:#00d4aa,color:#000
    style PW_SIGNED fill:#00d4aa,color:#000
    style MOVE_CONFIRMED fill:#00d4aa,color:#000
    style GRL fill:#7B1FA2,color:#fff
    style LL fill:#E91E8A,color:#fff
```

:::info

The config key `bitcoin_confirmation_threshold` (default `6`) stores the
Bitcoin confirmation threshold onchain. Hashi stores witness signatures
onchain so that any leader can reconstruct and re-broadcast the signed
Bitcoin transaction without MPC re-signing (for example, after leader
rotation, mempool eviction, or a Bitcoin reorganization).

**Limiter coordination.** The `LocalLimiter` on each committee node is a
deterministic projection of the onchain stream. Outside a reconcile (below),
its `next_seq` advances **only** when the node's object mirror sees a
`WithdrawalTransaction` become fully signed (the `finalize_withdrawal` write).
The finalize path uses `validate_consume` (read-only) to gate participation,
never to mutate state: the leader checks before it calls the guardian, and
each member checks again before it signs the finalize certificate. The
leader's flow only reaches `finalize_withdrawal()` after
`finalize_withdrawal_through_guardian` returns `Ok`, so seeing the transaction
become fully signed onchain is a sufficient proxy for the guardian having
acknowledged the request. The guardian advances its own `next_seq` when it
signs, so the local cache trails it while a withdrawal is in flight. On
startup, each node seeds its `LocalLimiter` through `GetGuardianInfo`, then
periodically reconciles against it, snapping back a cache that stalled or
drifted and adopting a new limiter policy after a guardian rotation.

:::

### Withdrawal flow summary

| Step | Actor           | Action                                       | Model Transformation                                                         |
| ---- | --------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | User            | User requests withdrawal                     | `Balance<BTC>` → `WithdrawalRequest` → `WithdrawalRequestQueue.requests`     |
| 2    | Committee       | Committee screens and approves request       | Members with a TRM API key screen it (Mainnet only); `approve_request()` records `approval_cert` on the request |
| 3    | Leader          | Leader commits withdrawal tx                 | `Balance<BTC>` burned, `WithdrawalTransaction` created in `.withdrawal_txns` |
| 4    | Committee (MPC) | MPC protocol signs Bitcoin transaction       | Committee signs each input through MPC; `commit_input_signatures()` stores the signatures onchain in chunks |
| 5    | Leader          | Leader checks its `LocalLimiter`             | `LocalLimiter::validate_consume(seq, ts, amt)` (read-only) before calling the guardian |
| 6    | Leader          | Leader BLS-certs `StandardWithdrawalRequest` | Aggregated cert over `(wid, seq, ts, utxos)`, the input to the guardian RPC |
| 7    | Guardian        | Guardian rate-limit check + enclave sig      | `StandardWithdrawal` RPC: verify cert → `consume(seq, ts, amt)` → enclave signatures |
| 8    | Leader          | Leader finalizes with guardian signatures    | Members re-run `validate_consume` and certify both signature sets; `finalize_withdrawal()` attaches the guardian signatures |
| 9    | Each node       | Each node advances its `LocalLimiter`        | Object mirror sees the tx become fully signed → `apply_consume(seq, ts, amt)` |
| 10   | Leader          | BTC transaction broadcast (and re-broadcast) | Signed tx reconstructed from onchain data, broadcast to Bitcoin              |
| 11   | Committee       | Committee signs confirmation certificate     | `CommitteeSignature` created after BTC tx confirmed                          |
| 12   | Leader          | Leader confirms withdrawal                   | `confirmed_timestamp_ms` set, input UTXOs marked spent; the leader's GC later moves the tx to `.confirmed_txns`, its requests to `.processed`, and the spent inputs to `spent_utxos` |

---

## What are the key Move models?

| Model                    | Location                                 | Description                                                            |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Balance<BTC>`           | User wallet                              | Wrapped BTC token on Sui                                               |
| `DepositRequest`         | `DepositRequestQueue.requests`, then `.processed` once confirmed | Deposit request with its approval cert and timestamps; deleted if it expires unconfirmed |
| `Utxo`                   | `UtxoPool`                               | Onchain representation of a Bitcoin UTXO                               |
| `WithdrawalRequest`      | `WithdrawalRequestQueue.requests`, then `.processed` once archived | User's withdrawal request with destination; `approval_cert` and `withdrawal_txn_id` mark approval and commitment |
| `WithdrawalTransaction`  | `WithdrawalRequestQueue.withdrawal_txns` | In-flight withdrawal tx (kept after confirmation until archived), stores inputs, outputs, and witness signatures |
| `WithdrawalTransaction`  | `WithdrawalRequestQueue.confirmed_txns`  | Confirmed withdrawal tx, moved here by the leader's archival GC (historical record) |
| `Bitcoin UTXO`           | Bitcoin Network                          | Actual unspent transaction output on Bitcoin                           |
| `Committee`              | `CommitteeSet`                           | BLS signing committee of Sui validators for an epoch                   |
| `CommitteeMember`        | `Committee.members`                      | Validator with public_key and voting weight                            |
| `CommitteeSignature`     | Built in the programmable transaction block (PTB) by `committee::new_committee_signature`; stored as `approval_cert` on requests | Aggregated BLS signature with signers bitmap |
| `CertifiedMessage<T>`    | Verified onchain                         | Message proven to have committee quorum support                        |

---

## Deposit

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/deposit.md

> How Hashi turns BTC sent to a deposit address into hBTC on Sui through the request, approve, confirm, and mint phases.

A deposit moves BTC from a user's Bitcoin wallet into the Hashi-managed UTXO
(unspent transaction output) pool, minting a corresponding amount of `hBTC`
into the user's account on Sui. The process has 4 phases:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Confirm] --> D[Mint]
```

The split between **Approve** and **Confirm** introduces a configurable
time-delay window (see
[`bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms`](config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms))
between the moment the committee certifies a deposit and the moment funds are
minted. This delay gives operators a chance to detect a faulty or fraudulent
approval and pause the service before the contract mints any `hBTC`.

## Request

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request]:::active --> B[Approve] --> C[Confirm] --> D[Mint]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

The user creates a Bitcoin transaction that sends BTC to a Hashi deposit
address. Each deposit address is a unique Taproot address derived from the
target destination address on Sui (see [Bitcoin Address Scheme](address-scheme.mdx)).
The deposit must meet the
[`bitcoin_deposit_minimum`](config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_minimum), which is never
below the dust minimum (`546 sats`), to avoid creating unspendable UTXOs on
Bitcoin.

After the Bitcoin transaction is broadcast, the user notifies Hashi by
constructing a `Utxo` and calling `hashi::deposit::deposit` on Sui.

You construct the `Utxo` from the Bitcoin transaction details:

```move
public fun utxo(
    utxo_id: UtxoId,
    amount: u64,
    derivation_path: Option<address>,
): Utxo

public fun utxo_id(
    txid: address,
    vout: u32,
): UtxoId
```

- `txid`: the 32-byte transaction hash in Bitcoin's internal byte order, the
  reverse of the hex txid that wallets and explorers show.
- `vout`: the output index within that transaction.
- `amount`: the deposit amount in satoshis.
- `derivation_path`: the Sui address used to derive the deposit address.

The user then submits it:

```move
entry fun deposit(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    utxo: Utxo,
    clock: &Clock,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

The function checks that the service is not paused (the contract accepts deposits
during a reconfiguration), that the deposit meets the minimum amount, and that
the UTXO is not already in the pool, active or spent. It then creates a
`DepositRequest` and places it in the deposit queue. Committee members start
monitoring Bitcoin for confirmation.

## Approve

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve]:::active --> C[Confirm] --> D[Mint]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

Committee members monitor the Bitcoin network for the deposit transaction. The
transaction must reach a sufficient number of block confirmations (see
[`bitcoin_confirmation_threshold`](config.mdx#bitcoin_confirmation_threshold))
before the committee considers it final. This guards against chain
reorganizations that could reverse a confirmed transaction. If the transaction
never reaches the threshold, for example because a reorg drops it, the
committee never approves the request. A request that the committee does not
confirm expires 24 hours after its creation, and the contract then deletes it;
the user can submit the UTXO again.

After confirmation, on Bitcoin Mainnet, each committee member with a TRM Labs
API key independently screens the deposit's Bitcoin transaction and Sui
recipient (see [Handling Sanctioned Addresses](sanctions.mdx)); other members
approve without screening. A member that rejects the deposit does not vote to
approve it.

After a node determines that a deposit request is both confirmed on Bitcoin
and passes its own screening checks, it communicates with the other members
of the Hashi committee and collects signatures from validators that agree to
approve the deposit. If a quorum of validators cannot agree to approve a
deposit, the node either retries the request later or ignores it
if invalid.

After the signatures reach a quorum, one validator submits the certificate onchain by
calling `hashi::deposit::approve_deposit`:

```move
entry fun approve_deposit(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    request_id: address,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

The function aborts while the service is paused or a reconfiguration is
pending, if the UTXO is already in the pool, or if the current committee has
already approved the request. Otherwise it verifies the committee certificate
against the current committee and records both the certificate and the
current clock timestamp on the request. The request remains in the deposit
queue, and the contract has not minted any `hBTC` yet.

## Confirm

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Confirm]:::active --> D[Mint]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

After approval, the deposit must wait through the configured time-delay
window (see
[`bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms`](config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms))
before anyone can confirm it. The window gives operators a chance to detect a
faulty or fraudulent approval and pause the service before the contract mints
funds. While the service is paused, the contract rejects both `approve_deposit`
and `confirm_deposit`, so pending approvals stay parked in the queue until the system is
unpaused, unless the request expires first. The 24-hour expiry described in
[Approve](#approve) counts from request creation, so it keeps running through
the time-delay window.

If the committee rotates before anyone confirms the deposit, the existing
approval becomes invalid and the new committee must re-approve the deposit,
which restarts the delay. The onchain `confirm_deposit` re-verifies
the stored certificate against the current committee, not the committee that
originally approved it.

After the delay has elapsed, any caller can call `hashi::deposit::confirm_deposit`:

```move
entry fun confirm_deposit(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    request_id: address,
    clock: &Clock,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

The function:

1. Aborts while the service is paused or a reconfiguration is pending, or if
   the UTXO is already in the pool (active or spent), before anything changes.
2. Re-verifies the stored committee certificate against the current committee.
3. Asserts that `approved_timestamp_ms + bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms <= now`.
4. Aborts if the request was never approved, the certificate no longer
   verifies, or the delay has not elapsed.

## Mint

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Confirm] --> D[Mint]:::active
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

After both checks in `confirm_deposit` pass, the function mints the
corresponding amount of `hBTC` and sends it to the Sui address in the UTXO's
`derivation_path` (a UTXO whose `derivation_path` is `None` mints nothing). The function adds the
deposited UTXO to the Hashi-managed UTXO pool, making it available
for future withdrawal coin selection.

---

## Withdraw

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/withdraw.md

> How Hashi turns hBTC on Sui back into native BTC through the request, approve, build, sign, and broadcast phases.

A withdrawal allows a user to redeem their `hBTC` on Sui for native BTC,
sent to a user-specified address on Bitcoin. The process has five phases:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]
```

## Who does what in a withdrawal?

1. **User**: calls `hashi::withdraw::request_withdrawal` with the `hBTC` and a
   Bitcoin destination address. Until the leader commits the request to a
   withdrawal transaction, the user can call
   `hashi::withdraw::cancel_withdrawal`, subject to a cooldown period.
2. **Committee**: approves the request with `hashi::withdraw::approve_request`.
   The leader then batches approved requests into a Bitcoin transaction and
   commits it with `hashi::withdraw::commit_withdrawal_tx`.
3. **Committee and Guardian**: the committee produces MPC signatures
   (`hashi::withdraw::commit_input_signatures`), the Guardian enclave produces
   the second signature, and the leader attaches it with
   `hashi::withdraw::finalize_withdrawal`.
4. **Leader and committee**: the leader broadcasts the signed transaction and,
   after the required confirmations, a committee member calls
   `hashi::withdraw::confirm_withdrawal`.

Beyond the request, the user's only optional actions are canceling and, if
the transaction gets stuck, fee bumping through child pays for parent (CPFP),
described in [Broadcast](#broadcast).

## How long does a withdrawal take?

The time from request to settlement depends mainly on these stages:

- **Batching**: the leader waits until a request has been waiting for roughly
  5 minutes since its submission, a threshold number of approved requests
  have accumulated, or the rate limiter can't fit the next request, whichever
  comes first. A request can wait longer if the Guardian's rate limiter is out
  of capacity, and Hashi never processes a request larger than the bucket's
  maximum capacity unless the limit increases (see [Build TX](#build-tx)).
- **One batch at a time**: the leader commits the next batch only after the
  previous one is fully signed.
- **Confirmations**: a committee member confirms the withdrawal after the
  transaction reaches
  the configured number of Bitcoin block confirmations
  ([`bitcoin_confirmation_threshold`](config.mdx#bitcoin_confirmation_threshold)).

## Request

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request]:::active --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

A user submits an onchain Sui transaction to request a withdrawal by calling
`hashi::withdraw::request_withdrawal`:

```move
entry fun request_withdrawal(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    clock: &Clock,
    btc: Balance<BTC>,
    bitcoin_address: vector<u8>,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

It is a private `entry` function, so you call it directly from a
programmable transaction block (PTB) rather than from other Move packages. A
PTB chains several commands in one transaction, and a later command can take
a value that an earlier one produced, so the `Balance<BTC>` can come from
earlier commands in the same PTB, such as `0x2::balance::redeem_funds` on the
sender's address balance.

- `btc`: the `hBTC` to withdraw, passed as a `Balance<BTC>`. Must be at least
  the [`bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum`](config.mdx#bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum).
- `bitcoin_address`: the destination witness program, either `P2WPKH` (20
  bytes) or `P2TR` (32 bytes). Hashi always pays a 32-byte program as `P2TR`.
  Because a `P2WSH` program is also 32 bytes, `P2WSH` destinations aren't
  supported.

The protocol enforces a minimum withdrawal amount to guarantee that every
request can produce a valid Bitcoin transaction even under worst-case fee
conditions. This minimum covers the worst-case miner fee (which pays for
both the user's transaction weight and opportunistic UTXO pool
consolidation) and the dust threshold for the user's output. See
[Fees](fees.mdx) for the full breakdown.

The contract stores the full `hBTC` amount with the request and places it in a
queue with a timestamp. The user can cancel their request at any point before
the leader commits it to a withdrawal transaction, including after approval,
subject to a cooldown period
([`withdrawal_cancellation_cooldown_ms`](config.mdx#withdrawal_cancellation_cooldown_ms)).
To cancel, the requester calls the private `entry` function
`hashi::withdraw::cancel_withdrawal`, which returns the refunded
`Balance<BTC>` for a later command in the same PTB, such as
`0x2::balance::send_funds` back to the sender.

## Approve

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve]:::active --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

On Bitcoin Mainnet, each committee member with a TRM Labs API key
independently screens the Bitcoin destination address and the requesting Sui
address (see [Handling Sanctioned Addresses](sanctions.mdx)); other members
approve without screening. A member that rejects the
request does not vote to approve it. If a quorum still approves, all members
must assist in completing the withdrawal.

Committee members communicate with each other to collect signatures to approve
the request. After the signatures reach a quorum, one member submits the certificate
onchain by calling `hashi::withdraw::approve_request`:

```move
entry fun approve_request(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    request_id: address,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
)
```

The function verifies the committee certificate and marks the request as
approved, so the leader can pick it up for transaction construction.

## Build TX

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX]:::active --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

The leader batches multiple approved requests into a single Bitcoin
transaction to amortize the fixed transaction overhead across users. The
leader waits for approved requests to buffer up before constructing a
transaction, until a request has been waiting for roughly 5 minutes since it
was submitted, a threshold number of approved requests have accumulated, or
the Guardian's token-bucket rate limiter (described below) can't fit the next
request, whichever comes first. This
balances latency for individual users against efficiency for the protocol.
The leader builds one batch at a time: it commits the next only after the
previous one is fully signed.

The leader takes approved requests oldest first and stops at the first one
that doesn't fit the current capacity of the Guardian's token-bucket rate
limiter, as tracked by the leader's own copy of it. That request and every
request behind it wait until capacity refills. The leader skips a request
larger than the bucket's maximum capacity every time, so Hashi never processes
it unless governance raises the limit; its owner can cancel it.

The leader then constructs an unsigned Bitcoin transaction:

1. **Coin selection**: select UTXOs from the pool to cover the total
   withdrawal amount (the user's withdrawn amount covers the miner fees).
   The coin selector might include extra inputs to opportunistically
   consolidate small UTXOs (see [Fees](fees.mdx)).
2. **Outputs**: one output per withdrawal request to each user's destination
   address, plus, when the inputs exceed the requested total, one change
   output back to a Hashi-controlled address.
3. **Fee calculation**: the leader estimates the miner fee through Bitcoin
   Core's `estimatesmartfee` RPC, floored at `3 sat/vB`, and deducts each
   user's share of the miner fee from their output. Validators independently verify
   that the fee is within acceptable bounds (at least `1 sat/vB`, at most 3x
   their own estimate).

The leader commits the resulting unsigned transaction and its txid onchain by
calling `hashi::withdraw::commit_withdrawal_tx`:

```move
entry fun commit_withdrawal_tx(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    request_ids: vector<address>,
    selected_utxos: vector<UtxoId>,
    outputs: vector<OutputUtxo>,
    txid: address,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
    r: &Random,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

The function verifies the committee certificate, burns the `hBTC` from each
request, locks the selected UTXOs in the pool, adds the change outputs to the
pool as pending UTXOs, and creates a pending withdrawal record that all
validators can independently verify.

## Sign

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign]:::active --> E[Broadcast]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

Signing is a two-step process matching the 2-of-2 Taproot script, which
requires both a committee (MPC) signature and a Guardian signature for each
input (see [Bitcoin Address Scheme](address-scheme.mdx)):

1. **MPC signature**: the committee runs the threshold Schnorr signing
   protocol (see [MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx)) to produce a signature for
   each input.
2. **Guardian signature**: once every input has an MPC signature, the leader
   sends the unsigned transaction and metadata, with a committee certificate,
   to the Guardian enclave, which checks the certificate and the request's
   timestamp, debits its rate limiter, and produces the second signature for
   each input.

The leader combines both signatures into the taproot script-path witness for
each input.

The leader commits the MPC signatures onchain in chunks, each under its own
committee certificate, by calling `hashi::withdraw::commit_input_signatures`:

```move
entry fun commit_input_signatures(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    withdrawal_id: address,
    indices: vector<u64>,
    signatures: vector<vector<u8>>,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
)
```

If a reconfiguration lands while a withdrawal is part-way through signing,
its still-unsigned inputs get fresh presignatures (see
[MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx)) from the new committee
(`hashi::withdraw::reallocate_presigs`); signatures already recorded stay.

The leader then attaches the Guardian signatures by calling
`hashi::withdraw::finalize_withdrawal`:

```move
entry fun finalize_withdrawal(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    withdrawal_id: address,
    guardian_signatures: vector<vector<u8>>,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
)
```

The function verifies a committee certificate over both signature sets and
marks the withdrawal fully signed. Each committee member re-checks the
withdrawal against its own copy of the rate limiter before signing that
certificate.

## Broadcast

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]:::active
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

The fully signed transaction is broadcast to the Bitcoin network. The
committee monitors the transaction until it reaches the configured number of
block confirmations (see
[`bitcoin_confirmation_threshold`](config.mdx#bitcoin_confirmation_threshold)).
Once confirmed, a committee member calls
`hashi::withdraw::confirm_withdrawal`:

```move
entry fun confirm_withdrawal(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    withdrawal_id: address,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
)
```

The function verifies the committee certificate, marks the withdrawal
confirmed and its input UTXOs spent, and promotes its change outputs from
pending to confirmed UTXOs. The withdrawal record stays in place until the
leader's garbage collection archives it with
`hashi::withdraw::archive_confirmed_withdrawals`, or, for a batch too large
for one transaction, `archive_withdrawal_requests` followed by
`finish_archive_withdrawal_txns`.

If a transaction gets stuck, CPFP handles fee bumping. Either the
withdrawal recipient spends their output with a high-fee child, or a later
withdrawal batch spends the stuck transaction's change UTXO and pays its fee
shortfall (see [Fees: stuck transactions](fees.mdx#stuck-transactions)).

---

## Reconfiguration

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/reconfiguration.md

> How the Hashi committee transfers MPC key shares between epochs through DKG or key rotation as Sui validators change.

Reconfiguration is one of the most important parts of the Hashi protocol,
because it is the step where the old committee shares key shares of the MPC
key with the new committee (see [MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx)).

The Hashi service monitors the Sui epoch change and immediately starts Hashi
reconfiguration after Sui's epoch change completes. During reconfiguration,
Hashi pauses in-progress operations (for example, processing of withdrawals).
The new committee resumes and processes them after reconfiguration completes.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Start Reconfig] --> B[DKG or Key Rotation] --> C[End Reconfig]
```

## How does a reconfiguration proceed?

On the happy path, a reconfiguration runs these steps in order:

1. A Hashi node detects a new Sui epoch while the Hashi epoch has not yet
   advanced to match.
2. Running nodes submit `hashi::reconfig::start_reconfig`; the first
   transaction to land forms the pending committee and sets the pending epoch
   change flag, which pauses deposit approval and confirmation, and withdrawal
   approval, commitment, and signing.
3. The new committee runs initial DKG (at genesis) or key rotation (in every
   later epoch), and each member ends with its `MpcOutput`.
4. Each member signs a `ReconfigCompletionMessage` with its BLS12-381 key, and
   nodes collect signatures until a quorum (2/3 of committee weight) produces
   an aggregate signature certificate.
5. On a key rotation only, nodes also collect the outgoing committee's
   signatures over a `CommitteeTransitionRequest`.
6. Within the same Sui epoch, a committee member submits `end_reconfig` (on a
   key rotation, together with `submit_committee_handoff` in the same
   transaction).
7. The chain verifies the certificate, advances the Hashi epoch, and clears
   the pending epoch change flag; deposits, and withdrawal approval and
   commitment, resume.
8. The new committee runs the presigning protocol; signing withdrawal inputs
   resumes once its presignatures are ready.

If Sui's epoch moves on before step 6 lands, [abort reconfig](#abort-reconfig)
resolves the pending reconfiguration instead.

## Start reconfig

Each Hashi node monitors Sui for epoch changes. When a new Sui epoch is
detected and the Hashi epoch has not yet advanced to match, the node knows
that it needs a reconfiguration. Every running node then submits
`hashi::reconfig::start_reconfig`, which is permissionless; the first
transaction to land forms the committee for Sui's current epoch:

```move
entry fun start_reconfig(
    self: &mut Hashi,
    sui_system: &SuiSystemState,
    ctx: &TxContext,
)
```

This sets a pending epoch change flag in the onchain state. Until
reconfiguration completes, the chain refuses deposit approval and
confirmation, and withdrawal approval, commitment, and signing
(`EReconfiguring`); users can still submit deposit and withdrawal requests,
which Hashi processes afterwards.
The active Sui validators that registered with Hashi and set their next-epoch
keys make up the new committee, leaving out any that
resigned or that governance ignored through an `IgnoreMember` proposal. Each
member's weight is its Sui voting power, and every threshold is a share of the
formed committee's total weight.

At genesis (the first Hashi epoch, when no MPC public key exists yet and the
committee must run initial DKG), the **launch switch**
additionally gates `start_reconfig`: it aborts until the publisher
has sent `hashi::finish_publish` (the `hashi launch` CLI command), which
finalizes the deploy configuration and hands the package `UpgradeCap` into
onchain custody. This gives the publisher explicit control over when (and
with which registered validators) the initial committee forms. After genesis
Hashi never consults the gate and applies no registration floor, because a
floor on a normal reconfig would let validators brick reconfiguration by
withholding registration.

## DKG or key rotation

The MPC key protocol runs among the new committee members. Which protocol
runs depends on whether this is the first Hashi epoch or a subsequent one:

- **Initial DKG**: if there is no existing MPC public key (the genesis epoch),
  the committee runs the distributed key generation protocol to produce a
  fresh master key.
- **Key rotation**: if an MPC public key already exists, the old committee
  redistributes its key shares to the new committee. The old committee
  members act as dealers and the new committee members act as receivers.

In both cases, each new member ends with an `MpcOutput`: its own key shares
and the MPC public key. See [MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx) for details.

Each committee member then signs a `ReconfigCompletionMessage` containing
the target epoch and the MPC public key using their BLS12-381 key. Nodes
collect signatures from each other through RPC until they reach a quorum (2/3 of
committee weight), producing a BLS aggregate signature certificate.
This ensures that a supermajority of the new committee agrees on the key
protocol output before the epoch transition finalizes onchain.

On a key rotation the outgoing committee must also approve the new one. Nodes
collect its signatures over a `CommitteeTransitionRequest` with the
`SignCommitteeTransition` RPC and submit that certificate through
`submit_committee_handoff`, in the same transaction as `end_reconfig`, which
does not activate a rotation without it. Initial DKG has no outgoing committee
and skips this step.

## End reconfig

A committee member submits the aggregate signature certificate onchain by
calling `hashi::reconfig::end_reconfig`:

```move
entry fun end_reconfig(
    self: &mut Hashi,
    mpc_public_key: vector<u8>,
    mpc_cert: CommitteeSignature,
    ctx: &TxContext,
)
```

The onchain contract verifies the certificate, commits the generated MPC
