public key if DKG ran (or verifies that the key remains unchanged from the
previous epoch), advances the Hashi epoch, and clears the pending epoch
change flag.

Completion must land inside the Sui epoch in which the reconfiguration formed.
`start_reconfig` pins the pending committee to Sui's epoch, and both
`submit_committee_handoff` and `end_reconfig` abort with
`EReconfigWindowClosed` once Sui's epoch has moved past it; from then on only
[abort reconfig](#abort-reconfig) can resolve the pending state. Each
submission is bound to its target. `end_reconfig` reads it from the
completion certificate's signing epoch; `submit_committee_handoff` takes it
as an explicit `epoch` argument, because the outgoing committee signs the
handoff certificate and its signing epoch is the source epoch. The signed
handoff message already binds the target, so the argument adds no security;
it lets the chain name the failure. Both entries abort with
`EWrongReconfigEpoch` when a different epoch is pending (the target was
aborted and a replacement has formed), before it checks any signature. It reports a
submission whose own target already activated as
`EReconfigAlreadyCompleted` (another node's `end_reconfig` won the race, which
the node treats as success), whether or not the next reconfiguration is
already pending; nothing pending otherwise is `ENotReconfiguring` (the target
was aborted). The contract stores handoffs by source epoch, and a replacement can form
from the same source epoch after an abort. So for a handoff, the submission
counts as its own target only if the handoff stored under the certificate's
signing epoch (the source epoch) names the submitted `epoch`. Nodes
key their retry-or-give-up decision on which of these fires.

| Error | Raised by | Condition | What it means for the node |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `EReconfigWindowClosed` | `submit_committee_handoff`, `end_reconfig` | Sui's epoch has moved past the pending committee's epoch | Only [abort reconfig](#abort-reconfig) can resolve the pending state |
| `EWrongReconfigEpoch` | `submit_committee_handoff`, `end_reconfig` | A different epoch is pending (checked before any signature) | The target was aborted and a replacement has formed |
| `EReconfigAlreadyCompleted` | `submit_committee_handoff`, `end_reconfig` | The submission's own target already activated, whether or not the next reconfiguration is pending | Another node's `end_reconfig` won the race; the node treats this as success |
| `ENotReconfiguring` | `submit_committee_handoff`, `end_reconfig` | Nothing is pending and the target did not activate | The target was aborted |

After the new epoch begins, the new committee initializes the signing state
for the epoch by running the presigning protocol to generate a batch of
presignatures needed for the threshold Schnorr signing protocol (see
[MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx)). Deposits, and withdrawal approval and
commitment, resume as soon as `end_reconfig` lands; signing withdrawal inputs
waits until the new committee's presignatures are ready.

## Abort reconfig

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Start Reconfig] --> B[DKG or Key Rotation] --> C[Abort Reconfig]:::active
    C --> A
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

Reconfiguration can fail after `start_reconfig` has committed the pending
committee but before `end_reconfig` can safely advance the Hashi epoch.
Examples include:

- The pending committee cannot complete initial DKG because too much
  registered stake is offline or misconfigured.
- Key rotation cannot complete because the old committee cannot supply enough
  valid resharing material to the new committee.
- The new committee completes the MPC protocol but cannot gather a threshold
  BLS certificate over a single `ReconfigCompletionMessage`.
- The MPC output is inconsistent with the onchain invariant that the threshold
  public key remains unchanged across key-rotation epochs.
- Stale or incorrect validator metadata, such as invalid endpoint, TLS, BLS,
  or encryption key updates, formed a bad pending committee.

In these cases, anyone can call the `reconfig::abort_reconfig` entry function
directly, naming the pending epoch to abort. It is deliberately not a
governance proposal and takes no vote: the committees that could vote on one
are exactly the parties a stalled reconfiguration puts in doubt. The pending
committee might never finish DKG or key rotation, and the same offline stake
that stalled the reconfiguration can strand a proposal gated on the outgoing
committee's quorum. Instead the abort is bound to objective onchain
conditions, all checked in the same transaction:

1. A reconfiguration is in progress, that is, a pending epoch change exists, and
   the named epoch is the pending one (a stale transaction cannot tear down a
   different reconfiguration).
2. The pending epoch is not Sui's current epoch. `start_reconfig` pins the
   pending committee's epoch to Sui's epoch at formation time, so while the
   two still match the reconfiguration is inside its window and might
   legitimately complete. Only once Sui's epoch has moved past the target is
   the reconfiguration stuck by definition: [end reconfig](#end-reconfig)
   refuses to land after the window, so completion and abort are mutually
   exclusive by Sui epoch and can never race each other.

The launch switch is not re-checked: a pending genesis committee can only
exist because `start_reconfig` passed it, and the package `UpgradeCap` it
looks for never leaves onchain custody.

When these hold, the call clears the pending epoch change, removes the pending
committee (discarding any committee handoff certificate it had collected), and
emits `ReconfigAborted` with the aborted epoch. The current Hashi epoch,
committee, and MPC public key remain unchanged. After genesis, normal
operations resume under the last committed committee; at genesis there is no
committee yet, so Hashi returns to its pre-genesis state. Either way the Hashi
epoch now lags Sui's, and a fresh `start_reconfig` forms a replacement
committee from the then-current validator set.

Nodes drive this themselves. When a node sees a checkpoint from a later Sui
epoch while a reconfiguration is still pending, it stops working on that
reconfiguration, submits the abort (the chain settles the race between nodes),
and submits the replacement `start_reconfig` as soon as the abort is
reflected. A node that observes an abort it did not submit, including one an
operator sent by hand with `hashi committee abort-reconfig`, starts the
replacement in the same way, as does a node that comes up to find Hashi's
epoch behind Sui's with nothing pending, whether or not it can rebuild its
own signing state for the lagging epoch. The CLI commands are therefore
fallbacks for when no node is doing this: `abort-reconfig` refuses up front
when nothing is pending or the pending epoch is still Sui's current epoch,
and `hashi committee start-reconfig` submits the replacement, refusing when
a reconfiguration is pending or Hashi is already on Sui's current epoch.

Governance can hold the replacement off. While the
[`reconfig_hold`](config.mdx#reconfig_hold) config flag is set through an
`UpdateConfig` proposal, `start_reconfig` aborts on chain, so no committee
can form and the last committed committee keeps serving deposits and
withdrawals; nodes see the flag and do not submit. A reconfiguration already
pending continues, and so does `abort_reconfig`, so the sequence for staying
on the last committed committee is to set the flag and then let the nodes abort the overrun
reconfiguration. Clearing the flag does not itself start a
replacement: nodes submit `start_reconfig` on a Sui epoch change, on an abort,
and at startup, and none of those is a config change, so the replacement waits
for the next Sui epoch change unless an operator runs
`hashi committee start-reconfig`.

Every abort observed on chain, whoever submitted it, increments the node
metric `hashi_reconfig_aborted_total`. An abort means a reconfiguration
stalled for an entire Sui epoch with deposits and withdrawals halted, so it is
worth alerting on and investigating even though the system recovers on its
own.

## Which CLI commands can operators run?

Nodes normally submit these transactions themselves; `abort-reconfig` and
`start-reconfig` are fallbacks for when no node is doing so.

| Command | What it does | Refuses when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hashi launch` | Sends `hashi::finish_publish` at genesis, finalizing the deploy configuration and handing the package `UpgradeCap` into onchain custody, which opens the launch switch | None |
| `hashi committee abort-reconfig` | Submits the abort for the pending reconfiguration | Nothing is pending, or the pending epoch is still Sui's current epoch |
| `hashi committee start-reconfig` | Submits the replacement `start_reconfig` | Governance holds reconfiguration (`reconfig_hold` is set), a reconfiguration is already pending, a committee already exists for Sui's current epoch, Hashi is already on Sui's current epoch, or the fullnode's Sui epoch is behind Hashi's |

---

## Governance Actions

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/governance-actions.md

> Proposal types that the Hashi committee uses to upgrade packages, enable or disable versions, and update onchain configuration.

Governance actions are each defined by a unique `Proposal<T>` type. Proposals
adjust protocol parameters, pause or unpause operations, or perform sensitive
operations like package upgrades.

## How does the committee vote on a proposal?

Each proposal type has its own threshold, which a quorum of validators must
reach by voting in support of the proposal. A proposal moves through these
steps:

1. A member of the current Hashi committee creates the proposal. Only members
   of the current committee can create proposals, and creating a proposal casts
   the creator's vote.
2. Committee members vote in support of the proposal until it reaches the
   threshold for its proposal type.
3. The proposal executes. The contract counts quorum against the committee in office
   when the proposal executes, so votes from members who left at a
   [reconfiguration](reconfiguration.mdx) no longer count. Executed proposals
   stay onchain.
4. A proposal expires 7 days after its creation; members can then no longer
   vote on or execute it, and anyone can delete it.

## What proposal types are available?

The following is the current set of available proposal types.

| Proposal | Effect | Abort codes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Upgrade` | Authorizes a package upgrade and records whether it is exclusive | None |
| `EnableVersion` | Re-enables a previously disabled package version | None |
| `DisableVersion` | Disables a package version | `EDisableCurrentVersion` |
| `UpdateConfig` | Updates existing keys in the instant config | `EInvalidConfigEntry`, `EProtectedConfigKey` |
| `UpdateEpochConfig` | Updates existing keys in the epoch config, including the MPC parameters | `EInvalidConfigEntry`, `EInconsistentMpcConfig` |
| `AddConfig` | Introduces new keys into the instant or epoch config | None |
| `IgnoreMember` | Flags a registered member as ignored, or clears the flag | None |
| `EmergencyPause` | Pauses or unpauses the bridge | None |

Configuration proposals target one of 2 stores: the instant config, where
new values apply when the proposal executes, and the epoch config, where the
next committee formed after execution receives the new values while the
active committee keeps its pinned copy.

## `Upgrade`

Authorizes a package upgrade and records whether it is exclusive. An exclusive
upgrade atomically disables all previous versions as the new package is
committed; a non-exclusive upgrade deliberately leaves them callable. Every
upgrade must make this classification explicitly. See
[Move Package Upgrades](move-upgrades.mdx) for the decision criteria and
validator rollout contract.

## `EnableVersion`

Re-enables a previously disabled package version, allowing the protocol to use
it again.

## `DisableVersion`

Disables a package version so the protocol can no longer use it. A version cannot
disable itself: executing the proposal through package version N refuses to
disable N (`EDisableCurrentVersion`). To disable a broken new version N:

1. Pick an older version that is still enabled.
2. Execute the `DisableVersion` proposal through that older version.

## `UpdateConfig`

Updates existing parameters in the instant config by key; the new values apply
when the proposal executes. The contract validates every entry when a member
creates the proposal and again when it executes, and the whole proposal aborts if any entry
fails: the key must already exist in the store with a value of the same type
(`EInvalidConfigEntry`), and the key must be governable. The guardian BTC
public key and the Bitcoin chain ID stay pinned for the deployment's lifetime,
and no config proposal can write them (`EProtectedConfigKey`).
Values themselves are otherwise not bounded onchain: a proposal needs a
supermajority of committee weight, and reviewing the proposed value is part of
voting. See [Configuration](config.mdx) for the keys and defaults.

This proposal also changes the guardian's URLs, with entries
that set `guardian_url` (the public endpoint) or `guardian_node_url` (the
endpoint nodes call) to a new string value. The URLs are the only guardian
settings governance can change: the guardian's BTC public key is immutable
once set, because rotating it would invalidate derived deposit addresses.
Executing the proposal changes the onchain value, but a running node keeps the
guardian client it already resolved from `guardian_node_url`, so you must
restart each node before it calls a new node URL. Nodes do not read
`guardian_url`.

## `UpdateEpochConfig`

Updates existing parameters in the epoch config by key, including the MPC
parameters, which must pass their range check (`EInvalidConfigEntry`). At
execution, `mpc_weight_reduction_allowed_delta` must also end up below
`mpc_max_faulty_in_basis_points` (`EInconsistentMpcConfig`). The next
committee formed after execution receives the new values; the active
committee keeps its pinned copy. This proposal also refuses the pinned keys
(the guardian BTC public key and the Bitcoin chain ID).

## `AddConfig`

Introduces new keys into the instant or epoch config, which is how a node-side
setting becomes governable without a package upgrade. The proposal is
insert-only: a key already present in the target store aborts, and the first
value fixes the key's type for later updates. The pinned key names cannot be
introduced into either store.

## `IgnoreMember`

Flags a registered member as ignored, or clears the flag. The next committee
formed leaves an ignored member out, so its weight drops out of every
threshold from then on; the current committee is never altered, and if a
reconfiguration is already pending the change lands one epoch later. The
member stays registered (no one can remove an ignored member as inactive), and
the same proposal type with the flag cleared re-admits it.

## `EmergencyPause`

Pauses or unpauses the bridge by setting the `paused` config flag. While
paused, the chain refuses new deposit and withdrawal requests and every
committee step that processes them, and each node refuses to sign for
deposits and withdrawals (not in the 1.0 releases). Users can still cancel
withdrawal requests, and reconfiguration and governance keep running. Anyone can
still broadcast a withdrawal fully signed before the pause, and a committee member
can still finish one the guardian already signed. The pause doesn't stop the
guardian. The two directions use different vote thresholds:

- **Pause:** `governance_emergency_pause_threshold_bps`, default 5% of committee
  weight. Pausing is deliberately cheap so a small fraction of the committee
  can quickly halt the system.
- **Unpause:** `governance_emergency_unpause_threshold_bps`, default two thirds.
  Unpausing requires a supermajority.

See [Configuration](config.mdx) for the keys and defaults. `paused` is also an
ordinary config key, so an `UpdateConfig` proposal can set or clear it at the
two-thirds threshold.

Aborting a stuck reconfiguration is deliberately **not** a proposal: the
committees that could vote on one are the parties a stalled reconfiguration
puts in doubt. It is a permissionless entry function gated on onchain state
instead; see [Abort Reconfig](reconfiguration.mdx#abort-reconfig). Holding
off the replacement that would otherwise follow is an `UpdateConfig` setting
[`reconfig_hold`](config.mdx#reconfig_hold), passed by the committee that is
still in service.

---

## Move Package Upgrades

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/move-upgrades.md

> How Hashi classifies Move upgrades as exclusive or non-exclusive, rolls out validator binaries, and retires old package versions safely.

Hashi package versions are separate callable Sui packages, but they operate on
the same shared `Hashi` object. Publishing a new package therefore does not make
an old package harmless. If an old entry function interprets shared state using
an obsolete invariant, it can overwrite or destroy work performed by the new
version.

The withdrawal v2 work exposed a concrete example. A request committed by v2
could remain in a location that v1 treated as cancellable. While v1 remained
enabled, its cancellation path could destroy that committed request, stranding
burned hBTC and locked UTXOs. This is why package publication and version
retirement sometimes need to be one atomic governance action. The Testnet v1 to
v2 plan below walks through the replay path that produces this state and how
the emergency pause closes it.

## When must an upgrade be exclusive or non-exclusive?

Every upgrade proposal must carry an **exclusive** or **non-exclusive** label in
its design and rollout plan. Reviewers should treat a missing classification as
an incomplete upgrade.

Use an **exclusive upgrade** when any of the following is true:

- The new version changes the meaning, location, or lifecycle of shared state.
- An old entry function could undo, overwrite, replay, or misclassify a new
  version's write.
- Safety depends on all callers using the new validation or authorization rule.
- No one has tested cross-version behavior directly.

Exclusive should be the default when there is doubt. It atomically replaces the
enabled-version set (the package versions that are still callable against the
shared `Hashi` object) with the newly committed version, so no transaction can
observe the new version enabled while an older version is still callable.

Use a **non-exclusive upgrade** only when retaining an older version is an
intentional compatibility feature. The review must explain why old and new
entry functions are safe against the same shared state and include direct
cross-version tests for state both versions can mutate. A desire to let old
validator binaries keep working is not, by itself, enough: binary rollout is an
operational concern and must not weaken an onchain safety invariant.

Each upgrade proposal goes through 4 stages: creation, voting to quorum,
execution, and finalization. The `upgrade::Upgrade` proposal records this
decision in its `exclusive`
field. Execution returns the Sui `UpgradeTicket` together with a non-droppable
authorization carrying the approved setting. Finalization consumes both in the
same programmable transaction, binding the committee vote to the version policy
that applies when the package commits. The CLI requires
`--exclusive true` or `--exclusive false`, and rejects an omission so the
classification cannot be an accidental default.

## How should validators coordinate a Move package upgrade?

An exclusive upgrade deliberately makes old binaries unable to perform normal
writes once they observe the upgrade checkpoint. An old binary does not contain
the code or ABI routing for the newest package, and the previous package is no
longer enabled. Updated Hashi nodes detect that they support no enabled package
version and halt autonomous mutations instead of falling back unsafely.

Use this sequence for every upgrade:

1. Build the exact Move package and record its digest in the proposal. Create
   exclusive proposals with `--package-path`, which verifies the package's
   `PACKAGE_VERSION` constant against the chain before proposing; the CLI
   refuses `--digest` for an exclusive upgrade unless
   `--allow-unverified-exclusive` explicitly acknowledges that the constant
   was not machine-checked.
2. Release a node binary that understands both the currently active package and
   the proposed package.
3. Restart validators one at a time. Each validator verifies healthy operation
   on the current package before casting its vote.
4. Confirm that upgraded validators represent at least two thirds of committee
   **weight**, not merely two thirds of node count.
5. Reach proposal quorum, then separately execute and publish the upgrade with
   `hashi proposal execute-upgrade <proposal-id> --package-path <dir>`, built
   from the same commit and `sui` binary as the proposal's digest. Votes never
   auto-publish a package.
6. Verify the package-upgrade checkpoint, enabled-version set, active routing,
   and validator health before resuming ordinary rollout work.

This ordering means the network retains quorum-capable updated software before
an exclusive publication causes old binaries to stop writing.

## What is the Testnet v1 to v2 upgrade plan?

The deployed Testnet v1 package only has the legacy `upgrade` proposal. That
proposal always leaves previous versions enabled, so it cannot make the first
v1-to-v2 transition atomic. Testnet carries no real funds, and the team accepts a small
race window for this one migration. Run the migration under the emergency
pause, which closes the withdrawal-replay surface described below; the
withdrawal queue does not need to drain first.

1. Create and fully vote the pause, v2 upgrade, and `DisableVersion(1)`
   proposals while v1 is active. Proposal creation permits targeting the
   current version; only execution rejects disabling it.
2. Execute the pause once the remaining proposals are near quorum. Governance
   entries are not pause-gated, so the remaining steps execute while paused.
3. Verify the bridge is still paused, then execute, publish, and finalize v2
   through the legacy v1 upgrade path (`hashi proposal execute-upgrade`).
4. Wait for that transaction to succeed and obtain the newly published v2
   package ID.
5. Immediately execute the already-approved disable-v1 proposal through the v2
   package. Pre-build this transaction so only the package ID needs filling.
6. Verify that v1 calls fail with `EVersionDisabled` and that validators route
   ordinary work through v2.
7. Create, vote, and execute the unpause.

Proposal execution checks only quorum, not the caller, so any quorum-complete
proposal is executable by any account. The strict ordering therefore votes the
unpause only after verifying `DisableVersion(1)`: a pre-voted unpause would
let an adversary unpause and commit through v2 in one transaction inside the
window. The Testnet migration relaxes this and pre-votes the unpause
alongside the other proposals, accepting the theoretical window: nothing of
value is at stake, the window is seconds wide, and the proposing operators
have executed every proposal to date. Any future migration that carries real
value must use the strict ordering; on Mainnet the question should not arise
at all, because exclusive upgrades replace the enabled set atomically and
leave no window to protect.

The upgrade and disable are necessarily two transactions. Do not submit them
concurrently: the network does not guarantee shared-object ordering, and
disable-v1 must execute through v2 after publication.

The pause is what makes the window between them safe for withdrawals.
Commitment and approval certificates bind no package version, so while both
versions are enabled an attacker can replay a live certificate through v2's
`commit_withdrawal_tx`. That commits the request in place, where v1's
pause-exempt `cancel_withdrawal` (it is not gated by the emergency pause and
checks only the `processed` bag) can
destroy it, burning the user's hBTC while releasing no BTC and wedging the
referencing withdrawal transaction forever. Every corrupting interleaving
requires such a v2 commit to land while v1 is still enabled.
`commit_withdrawal_tx` and `approve_request` honor the pause in both
packages, so holding the pause across the window means no transaction can
create that state, and the pause-exempt v1 cancel has nothing corruptible to
act on. In-flight withdrawals ride
through the flip without draining: committed batches sign, confirm, and
archive from their v1 locations, and approved or requested entries commit
v2-style afterward.

The pre-Mainnet tree ships this way already: the legacy module is gone,
the atomic proposal type carries the name `upgrade`, and it is the only upgrade path.
Mainnet begins with it from genesis.

---

## Rate Limiting Withdrawals

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/limiter.md

> Hashi enforces a token-bucket rate limit on withdrawal outflows through the Guardian to protect against vulnerabilities.

To protect against vulnerabilities or other exceptional scenarios, Hashi
implements a rate limiter on outflows through the Guardian.

## How does Hashi rate limit withdrawals?

A token-bucket rate limiter implements the limit, with two settings that
the operator sets when provisioning the Guardian: a maximum capacity in satoshis (a
Bitcoin denomination) and a refill rate in satoshis per second. Capacity
refills continuously up to the maximum.

| Setting | Unit | Set when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maximum capacity | satoshis | Guardian provisioning |
| Refill rate | satoshis per second | Guardian provisioning |

## How are withdrawal requests queued?

When a user wants to withdraw their `BTC` back to Bitcoin, they initiate a
withdraw request. Hashi tags every withdraw request with the timestamp of its
submission and places it in a queue to wait for processing.

## How does Hashi process queued withdrawals?

To process withdrawal requests, Hashi selects them from the queue and performs
a number of checks. If all checks pass and there is capacity, Hashi
works with the Guardian to sign and broadcast a Bitcoin transaction to satisfy
the requests. Hashi checks the limit at 3 points:

1. Before committing a batch, the leader checks it against its own copy of the
   Guardian's limiter, which every node seeds from the Guardian and keeps in
   step with it.
2. The Guardian enforces the limit itself when it co-signs.
3. Each committee member re-checks its own copy before certifying the signed
   transaction.

## What happens when a withdrawal exceeds the rate limit?

When a withdraw request would exceed the rate limit, Hashi waits to process
it until sufficient capacity refills. Hashi skips a request larger than the
limiter's maximum capacity until governance raises the limit; its owner can
cancel it.

## In what order are withdrawals processed?

Withdrawals are generally processed in first-in-first-out (FIFO) order, but
this is not a strict requirement, and there are some scenarios where Hashi
might process them out of order.

## Can users cancel a queued withdrawal?

The Sui address that initiated a withdrawal request can cancel that request
when both of the following hold:

- The
  [`withdrawal_cancellation_cooldown_ms`](config.mdx#withdrawal_cancellation_cooldown_ms)
  cooldown has passed.
- Hashi has not yet committed it to a Bitcoin withdrawal transaction.

---

## Handling Sanctioned Addresses

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/sanctions.md

> How Hashi committee members independently apply sanctions checks to deposits and withdrawals with their own TRM Labs accounts.

The decision to facilitate a transaction from or to Bitcoin must take into
account sanctioned addresses. For deposits, each validator screens a deposit
while it waits in the approval queue, before deciding whether to vote to
accept it; see [When sanctions checks apply](#when-sanctions-checks-apply)
and [Screening with TRM Labs](#screening-with-trm-labs).

## Checking if an address is sanctioned

Each member of the committee might have different risk tolerances or policies
for which set of addresses they do not want to serve. To accommodate different
validator preferences, the Hashi node software has a configurable mechanism
for determining whether to deny service to a particular address.

## Screening with TRM Labs

Each node operator screens with their own [TRM Labs](https://www.trmlabs.com)
account. To set up screening:

1. Create a TRM Labs account.
2. Create an API key in the TRM platform under **Settings > API Tokens**.
3. Set the key as `trm-api-key` in the node config.

Without a key, the node does not screen. TRM only covers Mainnet, so the node
ignores the key on other networks.

The following table lists what the node screens in each flow and which TRM API
it uses:

| Flow       | What the node screens                            | TRM API                                                  |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Deposit    | The Bitcoin transaction into the deposit address | Transaction Monitoring (`POST /public/v2/tm/transfers`)  |
| Deposit    | The Sui address credited with `hBTC`             | Wallet Screening (`POST /public/v2/screening/addresses`) |
| Withdrawal | The Bitcoin destination address                  | Wallet Screening                                         |
| Withdrawal | The Sui address that requested the withdrawal    | Wallet Screening                                         |

A node does not vote for a deposit or withdrawal when:

- TRM attributes a screened address itself (risk type `OWNERSHIP`) to a
  category scored High or Severe. Exposure only through counterparties or
  intermediaries does not count.
- The deposit's transfer raises an alert at High or Severe.
- TRM cannot screen the transfer, or rejects the request.

The node logs why. The leader asking for its vote learns only that the node's
sanctions check has not approved the request.

Transaction Monitoring is asynchronous. A node waits up to 10 seconds for TRM
to finish screening a deposit's transfer; if TRM is still processing it, the
node declines the deposit for now and the leader retries on the next Bitcoin
block. Timeouts, rate limits and TRM server errors are also retried, and the
node does not vote in the meantime. TRM can still alert on a transfer after
the committee approves the deposit; hashi does not revisit an approval.

## When sanctions checks apply

**Deposits**: When a user submits a deposit request, their request sits in a
queue or waiting room until the validators vote on accepting that deposit
and minting an appropriate amount of `hBTC`. Sanctions checking happens at
the time a validator decides whether to vote for accepting a deposit. If a
validator decides that it does not want to service that deposit, it does not
vote for it and ignores that the deposit exists. If a quorum decides to
accept a deposit that a particular validator did not want to accept, per
protocol the validator must recognize (and subsequently make use of) the
deposited BTC.

**Withdrawals**: When a user submits a withdraw request, their request sits
in a queue or waiting room until the validators pick it up for processing.
Before selecting a request for processing, the validators vote on approving
the request. One of the required checks as part of voting for approval is
performing sanctions checking. After a quorum of validators has voted to
approve a request, a node can pick it up for processing. If a quorum decides
to approve a request for processing, per protocol all validators must
assist in driving the request to completion.

## Tainted UTXOs

The Hashi protocol implements rigorous sanctions enforcement, but enforcement
is ultimately best-effort. A quorum of validators might accept a deposit that
one validator preferred to not accept, or a previous committee accepted a
deposit that the current committee would have rejected. In either case, after
Hashi accepts a UTXO into its pool, the protocol treats it as its own, and
it must be available during coin selection to process withdraw requests.

---

## Fees

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/fees.md

> How Hashi charges miner fees on withdrawals, enforces fee bounds, and handles stuck transactions.

Hashi charges no protocol fee. Deposits are free, and every withdrawal
pays only the Bitcoin **miner fee** required to get the transaction
confirmed onchain.

## Fee parameters at a glance

| Value | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bitcoin_deposit_minimum` | 30,000 sats (initial) | Configurable minimum deposit |
| `bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum` | 30,000 sats | Set by governance; Hashi derives `worst_case_network_fee` from it |
| `worst_case_network_fee` | 29,454 sats | Derived: `max(bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum, 547) - 546` |
| `DUST_RELAY_MIN_VALUE` | 546 sats | Bitcoin's dust threshold for the user's output |
| `withdrawal_fee_conf_target` | 3 blocks | At most 12 |
| `withdrawal_min_fee_rate_sat_vb` | 3 sat/vB | Fee-rate floor, configurable per node |
| Mainnet fee-rate cap | 100 sat/vB | Applies to the estimate before the floor |
| Signet fee-rate cap | 9 sat/vB | Applies to the estimate before the floor |

## Deposits

Deposits are free. They must meet the configurable
`bitcoin_deposit_minimum` (initially `30,000 sats`).

## Withdrawal fees

The only fee a user pays on withdrawal is the **miner fee**, the actual
Bitcoin transaction fee required for onchain confirmation. This is not a
fixed value. It depends on the current network fee rate and the
transaction's weight. The user pays this fee through a reduction in their
withdrawal output amount. There is no protocol fee.

### Why the user pays the miner fee

The UTXO pool belongs to the protocol. If the pool absorbed miner fees,
every withdrawal would shrink the pool by more than the withdrawn
amount, effectively socializing costs across all future users. Shifting
the miner fee to the withdrawing user keeps the pool whole: the
invariant `input_total = user_output + change` holds, so the change
output that returns to the pool is undiminished.

### Withdrawal minimum

The protocol enforces a minimum withdrawal amount to guarantee
that every request can produce a valid Bitcoin transaction even under
worst-case fee conditions. Governance sets `bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum`
directly (default 30,000 sats), and Hashi derives `worst_case_network_fee`
from it, so the 2 always satisfy:

```
bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum = worst_case_network_fee + DUST_RELAY_MIN_VALUE
```

- `worst_case_network_fee` is the maximum miner fee the protocol ever
  charges (see below).
- `DUST_RELAY_MIN_VALUE` (`546 sats`) ensures the user's output remains
  above Bitcoin's dust threshold after the miner fee deduction.

A user who withdraws exactly the minimum receives, in the worst case, a
`546 sats` output. In practice, actual miner fees are usually well below
the worst case, so the user receives more.

## Fee rate estimation

Hashi obtains the current fee rate from the connected Bitcoin Core node
through `estimatesmartfee` in `ECONOMICAL` mode, targeting confirmation
within `withdrawal_fee_conf_target` blocks (default `3`, around 30
minutes; at most `12`). Longer targets would read Core's day- and
week-long estimation horizons, which lag the fee market.

If Bitcoin Core has no estimate, for example while its estimator warms up
after a restart, the leader doesn't build withdrawal transactions and
validators don't sign them. Only regtest, which has no fee market, falls
back to `1 sat/vB`.

Hashi then floors the estimated fee rate at 3 sat/vB (configurable per node
with `withdrawal_min_fee_rate_sat_vb`). The onchain
`worst_case_network_fee` bounds each user's share of the miner fee: while
a batch's share would exceed it, the leader waits for fees to fall or for
more requests to share them, rather than broadcasting a transaction that
would sit unconfirmed.

On Mainnet Hashi also caps the estimate at 100 sat/vB before the floor
applies. That is far above what blocks usually charge, but fee spikes have
passed it for days at a time, as in December 2023. Hashi can't replace a signed withdrawal
with a higher-fee version, so one priced at the cap during
a spike stays unconfirmed until fees fall back.

Signet's cap is lower. Its blocks rarely fill, but Bitcoin Core's
estimate there follows the few relayed transactions that pay hundreds of
sat/vB, so on Signet Hashi caps the estimate at 9 sat/vB before the floor
applies.

Raising that floor on the leader alone only helps so far. Validators
derive their ceiling from their own floor and estimate, so they reject a fee more than
3x above what they see; operators must configure a larger rescue
across the fleet.

## Worst-case network fee

Every withdrawal must cover not just its own onchain footprint
but also a share of UTXO pool maintenance. At minimum, a withdrawal must
pay for the fixed transaction overhead, its own recipient output, and a
change output back to the pool. The additional headroom allows the coin
selector to consolidate many small UTXOs into fewer large ones during
normal withdrawal traffic. This opportunistic consolidation (UTXO
smashing) keeps the pool healthy without requiring dedicated consolidation
transactions.

Hashi derives the worst-case miner fee per withdrawal from the
governance-configured `bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum` parameter:

```
worst_case_network_fee = bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum - DUST_RELAY_MIN_VALUE
```

With defaults: `30,000 - 546 = 29,454` sats.

The actual miner fee is usually well below the worst case. Users are
charged only for the real transaction weight, not the worst-case
budget. The difference stays in the user's output.

## Transaction validation fee bounds

When validators verify a proposed withdrawal transaction, they check
the fee against three bounds:

- **Floor**: the fee must be at least `1 sat/vB` (the minimum relay fee),
  or the Bitcoin network does not propagate the transaction.
- **Ceiling**: the fee must not exceed 3x the validator's own fee
  estimate for the same transaction weight, including any CPFP deficit
  its unconfirmed ancestors owe (see
  [Stuck transactions](#stuck-transactions)). This prevents a malicious leader from
  overpaying fees to extract value from users.
- **Per-user cap**: the per-user share of the miner fee must not exceed
  the worst-case network fee computed from the onchain config. This
  ensures the Move contract's upfront minimum calculation was
  sufficient.

## Stuck transactions

Hashi does not attempt to replace stuck transactions with higher-fee
replacements (Replace-By-Fee, or RBF). Instead, if a transaction is not
confirmed within a reasonable time, fee bumping relies on CPFP
(Child Pays For Parent):

- The withdrawal recipient can spend their output with a high-fee child
  transaction.
- Hashi can spend the change UTXO that returned to the pool, which also
  bumps the parent.

---

## User Flows

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/user-flows.md

> End-to-end deposit and withdrawal flows for users moving BTC between Bitcoin and Sui through Hashi.

`hashi` has 2 main user flows: deposits, which
turn `BTC` into `hBTC` on Sui, and withdrawals, which turn `hBTC` back into
native `BTC` at a Bitcoin address you specify. For the phase-by-phase details,
see [Deposit](deposit.mdx) and [Withdraw](withdraw.mdx).

:::info
The only coin the Hashi protocol creates is `hBTC`, the Bitcoin-backed asset it
mints on deposit. There is no `$HASHI` token: Hashi has no governance, utility,
or airdrop token, and committee members govern the protocol by voting onchain
with their validator stake weight. Treat any `$HASHI` token offering, presale,
or airdrop as an imitation.
:::

## Deposit flow

To use `BTC` on Sui (for example, as collateral for a loan), you must
deposit your `BTC` to a Hashi Bitcoin address, spendable by the MPC committee
together with the Guardian. Your own wallet keys do not control the deposit
address. To try the flow without real `BTC`, see
[Try a deposit on Testnet](hbtc/deposit.mdx#try-a-deposit-on-testnet).

<div style={{zoom: 1.5}}>

```mermaid
---
title: Deposit Flow
config:
  sequence:
    diagramMarginX: 0
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber

    participant User
    participant Hashi as Sui / Hashi
    participant Bitcoin

    User    ->>     Bitcoin:    Deposit native BTC
    User    ->>     Hashi:      Notify hashi of deposit
    Hashi   ->>     Bitcoin:    Query for deposit
    Hashi   ->>     Hashi:      Quorum agreement on deposit
    Hashi   ->>     User:       hBTC sent to User
```

</div>

### BTC deposit address

Every Sui address has its own unique Hashi Bitcoin deposit address. See
[Bitcoin Address Scheme](address-scheme.mdx) for the full derivation
details.

### How to deposit BTC

After you determine your deposit address, you can initiate a deposit to
Hashi.

1. Broadcast a Bitcoin transaction depositing `BTC` (at least
   [`bitcoin_deposit_minimum`](config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_minimum)) into your
   unique deposit address.
1. Notify Hashi of the deposit by submitting a transaction to Sui that
   includes the deposit transaction ID.
1. Hashi nodes query Bitcoin and watch for confirmation of the deposit
   transaction.
1. Hashi nodes communicate, waiting until a quorum has confirmed the deposit
   (after
   [`bitcoin_confirmation_threshold`](config.mdx#bitcoin_confirmation_threshold)
   block confirmations).
1. After the
   [`bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms`](config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms)
   window, Hashi confirms the deposit onchain, minting the equivalent amount of
   `hBTC` and transferring it to your Sui address. You can then immediately
   use the `hBTC` to interact with a DeFi protocol. For example, you can use
   the `hBTC` as collateral for a loan in `USDC`.

For step-by-step instructions with the CLI or the SDK, see
[Deposit BTC](hbtc/deposit.mdx). For a detailed breakdown of each phase, see
[Deposit](deposit.mdx).

## Withdraw flow

After you decide you want your `BTC` back on Bitcoin (for example, after you
pay off your loan), you can initiate a withdrawal.

<div style={{zoom: 1.5}}>

```mermaid
---
title: Withdraw Flow
config:
  sequence:
    diagramMarginX: 0
---
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber

    participant User
    participant Hashi as Sui / Hashi
    participant Bitcoin

    User    ->>     Hashi:   Request withdrawal
    Hashi   ->>     Hashi:   Craft and sign Bitcoin transaction (MPC and Guardian)
    Hashi   ->>     Bitcoin: Broadcast transaction
```

</div>

### How to withdraw BTC

1. You send a transaction to Sui with the amount of `hBTC` you want to
   withdraw (at least
   [`bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum`](config.mdx#bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum)) and
   the P2WPKH or P2TR Bitcoin address you want to withdraw to.
1. Hashi picks up the withdrawal request and crafts a Bitcoin transaction
   that sends the requested `BTC` (minus fees) to the provided Bitcoin
   address, then signs it with the MPC committee and the Guardian.
1. The transaction is broadcast to the Bitcoin network.

For step-by-step instructions with the CLI or the SDK, see
[Withdraw BTC](hbtc/withdraw.mdx) and [Cancel a Withdrawal](hbtc/cancel.mdx).
For a detailed breakdown of each phase, see [Withdraw](withdraw.mdx).

---

## Deposit BTC

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/hbtc/deposit.md

> How to deposit BTC into Hashi and receive hBTC on Sui using the Hashi CLI or the TypeScript SDK, from deriving your deposit address to tracking the mint.

To use BTC on Sui, you deposit it with Hashi and receive `hBTC`, a fungible
`Coin<BTC>`, at your Sui address. You can make a deposit with the Hashi CLI or
with the TypeScript SDK. Both follow the same 3 steps: derive your deposit
address, send BTC to it, and record the funding transaction on Sui. This page
covers the steps. For what the committee does with your request, see the
[Deposit](../deposit.mdx) lifecycle.

<Tabs className="tabsHeadingCentered--small">
<TabItem value="prereq" label="Prerequisites">
- [x] A Sui address funded with SUI for gas, and its private key in one of the [accepted key formats](../validators/keys.mdx#operator-key-day-to-day-signing).
- [x] A Bitcoin wallet holding BTC on the network that matches your Sui network. Hashi pairs Sui Mainnet with Bitcoin Mainnet and Sui Testnet with Bitcoin Signet. See the [Networks](../reference/networks.mdx) table.
- [x] For the CLI: a `hashi` binary built as described in [Software dependencies](../validators/prerequisites.mdx#software-dependencies) and a CLI config file from [CLI config](../validators/configuration.mdx#cli-config).
- [x] For the SDK: a Node.js project with `@mysten/hashi` and `@mysten/sui` installed as described in [TypeScript SDK](../ts-sdk.mdx).
</TabItem>
</Tabs>

## Before you deposit

Keep the following rules in mind:

- **Minimum amount:** Each deposit must be at least
  [`bitcoin_deposit_minimum`](../config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_minimum). Hashi
  rejects smaller deposits onchain.
- **Your keys do not control the deposit address:** The address is spendable
  only by the Hashi committee together with the Guardian. See
  [Bitcoin Address Scheme](../address-scheme.mdx).
- **One address per Sui address:** Hashi derives the deposit address from the
  Sui address that receives the `hBTC`. Sending to the wrong address credits
  the wrong Sui account.
- **Record the deposit yourself:** Hashi does not scan Bitcoin for incoming
  funds. It mints `hBTC` only after you record the funding transaction on
  Sui.

## Deposit with the CLI

CLI global options such as `-c` belong after the first-level subcommand, so
`-c` goes after `deposit`. See
[Global options](../reference/cli.mdx#global-options) for the full
rule and the environment variables that replace the flags.

##### Step 1: Generate your deposit address

Run the following command with the Sui address that receives the `hBTC`:

```bash
hashi deposit -c hashi-cli.toml generate-address --recipient 0x<sui-address>
```

The command derives a Taproot address from the onchain MPC public key and the
Guardian key. The result is the same every time for the same Sui address.

##### Step 2: Send BTC to the address

Send at least the minimum deposit amount to the address from any Bitcoin
wallet. Record the Bitcoin transaction ID (txid) and the output index (vout) that
paid your deposit address.

##### Step 3: Record the deposit on Sui

Tell Hashi about the funding transaction:

```bash
hashi deposit -c hashi-cli.toml request --txid <btc-txid> --outputs '[[<vout>, <amount-sats>]]' --recipient 0x<sui-address>
```

If you omit `--outputs`, the CLI looks the transaction up through the Bitcoin
RPC endpoint in your CLI config and finds the outputs that paid the deposit
address. If one funding transaction paid the address on several outputs, list
them all in `--outputs` and the CLI batches them into one Sui transaction.

The command prints a deposit request ID. Keep it for the next step.

##### Step 4: Track the deposit

Check the request and your balance:

```bash
hashi deposit -c hashi-cli.toml status <request-id>
hashi balance -c hashi-cli.toml 0x<sui-address>
```

Expect to wait. The committee waits for
[`bitcoin_confirmation_threshold`](../config.mdx#bitcoin_confirmation_threshold)
Bitcoin blocks, then approves the deposit, then waits through the
[`bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms`](../config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms)
window before minting. See
[How long does a deposit take?](faq.mdx#how-long-does-a-deposit-take) for the
defaults.

## Deposit with the TypeScript SDK

The SDK attaches to a Sui client and exposes every Hashi method under
`client.hashi.*`. Install it and create a client as described in
[TypeScript SDK](../ts-sdk.mdx#setup). The SDK page also lists which Sui
networks the SDK supports.

##### Step 1: Derive the deposit address and record the deposit

The following example derives the deposit address for the signer's Sui
address and, after you send BTC to it, records the funding transaction on Sui:

```ts
const recipient = signer.toSuiAddress();

// 1. Get the deposit address.
const btcAddress = await client.hashi.generateDepositAddress({
	suiAddress: recipient,
});

// 2. Send BTC to `btcAddress` from any wallet, then collect the
//    funding tx's display-order txid and the vout that paid the
//    deposit address. (Display-order = the form mempool.space and
//    `bitcoin-cli` show — the SDK reverses internally.)

// 3. Record the deposit on Sui.
const result = await client.hashi.deposit({
	signer,
	txid: '0x<64-hex display-order txid>',
	utxos: [{ vout: 0, amountSats: 100_000n }],
	recipient,
});

if (result.$kind !== 'Transaction') {
	throw new Error(`deposit failed: ${JSON.stringify(result.FailedTransaction)}`);
}
// `hBTC` lands in `recipient`'s balance once the committee confirms.
```

Pass every output that paid the deposit address in `utxos`. The SDK batches
them into one atomic Sui transaction.

:::tip

Before you submit, check that the outputs are not already recorded. Submitting
a consumed UTXO aborts onchain.

```ts
const results = await client.hashi.view.findUsedUtxos([
	{ txid: '0x<64-hex display-order txid>', vout: 0 },
]);
// results[0]: { utxoId, inActivePool, inSpentPool, isUsed }
```

:::

##### Step 2: Track the deposit

Use the transaction digest to check status once or to wait for a terminal
state:

```ts
const digest = result.Transaction?.digest;

// One-shot status check — returns null if the digest has no Hashi event.
const deposit = await client.hashi.view.depositStatus(digest);
// deposit?.status: "pending" | "confirmed" | "expired" | "unknown"
// deposit?.approvalTimestampMs — when the committee approved (null until approved)
// deposit?.confirmableAtMs — earliest mint time = approval + bitcoinDepositTimeDelayMs
//                            (null until approved)
```

```ts
const info = await client.hashi.waitForDeposit(digest, {
	intervalMs: 15_000, // default
	signal: AbortSignal.timeout(600_000), // optional cancellation
});
```

##### Step 3: Check your hBTC balance

```ts
const { totalBalance, coinObjectCount } = await client.hashi.view.balance(signer.toSuiAddress());
// totalBalance — hBTC in satoshis; coinObjectCount — number of coin objects held.
```

## Try a deposit on Testnet

Hashi's Testnet deployment uses Bitcoin Signet, so a test deposit needs Signet
BTC. Signet coins have no value, and you cannot buy or mine them in any
practical sense. You get them from a faucet.

:::caution

The Signet faucets below are third-party services that the Hashi team does not
operate or verify. Availability, rate limits, and URLs change without notice,
and this page makes no guarantee that any of them work at the time you read
it. Never send real BTC to a Signet faucet or a Signet address.

:::

Commonly used public faucets for the default Signet network include
[signetfaucet.com](https://signetfaucet.com/) and its alternate at
[alt.signetfaucet.com](https://alt.signetfaucet.com/). Confirm that a faucet
serves default Signet before using it. Some communities run custom signets
whose coins are not valid on the network Hashi's Testnet uses. Your own Signet
node cannot create spendable coins for you, because a central authority signs
Signet blocks.

For the CLI, set `network = "signet"` under `[bitcoin]` in `hashi-cli.toml`,
or pass `--btc-network signet`. The CLI otherwise assumes regtest and derives
a `bcrt1` address. Then follow the CLI steps above. Expect to wait for several
Signet blocks between recording the deposit and seeing `hBTC` in your balance.

---

## Withdraw BTC

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/hbtc/withdraw.md

> How to redeem hBTC on Sui for native BTC using the Hashi CLI or the TypeScript SDK, including destination address rules, the miner fee, and how to track the withdrawal.

To move BTC back to Bitcoin, you submit a withdrawal request on Sui that burns
your `hBTC` and names the Bitcoin address that receives the BTC. You can make
the request with the Hashi CLI or with the TypeScript SDK. This page covers the
steps. For what the committee and the Guardian do with your request, see the
[Withdraw](../withdraw.mdx) lifecycle.

<Tabs className="tabsHeadingCentered--small">
<TabItem value="prereq" label="Prerequisites">
- [x] A Sui address holding `hBTC` and funded with SUI for gas, and its private key in one of the [accepted key formats](../validators/keys.mdx#operator-key-day-to-day-signing).
- [x] A Bitcoin address you control on the network that matches your Sui network. See the [Networks](../reference/networks.mdx) table.
- [x] For the CLI: a `hashi` binary built as described in [Software dependencies](../validators/prerequisites.mdx#software-dependencies) and a CLI config file from [CLI config](../validators/configuration.mdx#cli-config).
- [x] For the SDK: a Node.js project with `@mysten/hashi` and `@mysten/sui` installed as described in [TypeScript SDK](../ts-sdk.mdx).
</TabItem>
</Tabs>

## Before you withdraw

Keep the following rules in mind:

- **Minimum amount:** Each request must be at least
  [`bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum`](../config.mdx#bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum).
  The minimum guarantees that the request can pay the worst-case miner fee and
  still leave an output above Bitcoin's dust threshold.
- **Accepted destination addresses:** Hashi pays `P2WPKH` (bech32, `bc1q` on
  Mainnet) and `P2TR` (bech32m, `bc1p` on Mainnet) addresses. It does not
  support `P2WSH` or legacy address types. The address must belong to the
  Bitcoin network that matches your Sui network.
- **You pay the miner fee:** Hashi charges no protocol fee, but it deducts the
  Bitcoin miner fee from your output. The amount of BTC you receive is less
  than the `hBTC` you burn. See [Fees](../fees.mdx) for how Hashi bounds the
  fee.
- **Withdrawals queue:** Your request waits for committee approval, batching
  with other requests, and capacity in the Guardian's rate limiter. See
  [How long does a withdrawal take?](faq.mdx#how-long-does-a-withdrawal-take).

## Withdraw with the CLI

CLI global options such as `-c` belong after the first-level subcommand, so
`-c` goes after `withdraw`. See
[Global options](../reference/cli.mdx#global-options).

##### Step 1: Submit the request

Run the following command with the amount in satoshis and your destination
address:

```bash
hashi withdraw -c hashi-cli.toml request --amount <sats> --btc-address <addr>
```

The command burns the `hBTC` from your address, places the request in the
withdrawal queue, and prints the withdrawal request ID. Keep the ID. You need
it to check status and to cancel.

##### Step 2: Track the request

Check one request, or list all of them:

```bash
hashi withdraw -c hashi-cli.toml status <request-id>
hashi withdraw -c hashi-cli.toml list --json
```

The request moves through the states Requested, Approved, Processing, Signed,
and Confirmed. After Hashi commits the Bitcoin transaction, the status includes
its txid, which you can follow in any Bitcoin explorer.

## Withdraw with the TypeScript SDK

The SDK attaches to a Sui client and exposes every Hashi method under
`client.hashi.*`. Install it and create a client as described in
[TypeScript SDK](../ts-sdk.mdx#setup).

##### Step 1: Check fees and limiter capacity

Before you submit, you can read the worst-case miner fee, the onchain minimum,
and whether the Guardian's rate limiter can sign your amount right now:

```ts
// Withdrawal: worst-case BTC network fee + on-chain minimum. Pass a sender
// to also get a dry-run gas estimate.
const fees = await client.hashi.view.withdrawalFees(signer.toSuiAddress());
// { worstCaseNetworkFeeSats, withdrawalMinimumSats, gasEstimateMist }
```

```ts
// Can the guardian sign a 50,000-sat withdrawal right now?
const check = await client.hashi.guardian.canWithdraw(50_000n);
// { allowed, availableNowSats, estimatedWaitSecs }
```

##### Step 2: Submit the request

The SDK decodes the destination address as bech32 or bech32m and checks that
it matches the client's Bitcoin network before signing:

```ts
const result = await client.hashi.requestWithdrawal({
	signer,
	amountSats: 50_000n,
	bitcoinAddress: 'tb1q…', // P2WPKH on signet/testnet, or `tb1p…` for P2TR
});

if (result.$kind !== 'Transaction') {
	throw new Error(`request failed: ${JSON.stringify(result.FailedTransaction)}`);
}

// Pull the request id out of the WithdrawalRequested — needed if
// you later want to cancel.
const evt = result.Transaction.events?.find((e) =>
	e.eventType.endsWith('::withdrawal_queue::WithdrawalRequested'),
);
const requestId = (evt as { json?: { request_id?: string } } | undefined)?.json?.request_id;
```

Keep `requestId` if you might [cancel the withdrawal](cancel.mdx).

##### Step 3: Track the request

Use the transaction digest to check status once or to wait for a terminal
state:

```ts
const withdrawal = await client.hashi.view.withdrawalStatus(digest);
// withdrawal?.status: "Requested" | "Approved" | "Processing"
//                     | "Signed" | "Confirmed" | "cancelled"
```

```ts
const wInfo = await client.hashi.waitForWithdrawal(digest);
// wInfo.btcTxid is populated once the committee commits the Bitcoin tx.
```

## If the transaction is slow to confirm

Hashi does not replace a slow Bitcoin transaction with a higher-fee version.
If your withdrawal sits in the mempool, you can speed it up yourself by
spending your output with a higher-fee child transaction, which pays for the
parent. See [Stuck transactions](../fees.mdx#stuck-transactions).

---

## Cancel a Withdrawal

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/hbtc/cancel.md

> When you can cancel a pending Hashi withdrawal and how to do it with the CLI or the TypeScript SDK to get your hBTC back.

A withdrawal request waits in a queue before Hashi commits it to a Bitcoin
transaction. While it waits, you can cancel it and get your `hBTC` back. This
page explains when a cancellation succeeds and how to submit one with the
Hashi CLI or the TypeScript SDK.

## When you can cancel

The onchain contract enforces 3 conditions. All of them must hold:

- **You made the request:** Only the Sui address that submitted the request
  can cancel it.
- **Hashi has not committed it yet:** The request must still be in the
  Requested or Approved state. After the committee commits the request to a
  Bitcoin transaction, Hashi burns the `hBTC` and the withdrawal completes on
  Bitcoin. You cannot cancel it.
- **The cooldown has passed:** At least
  [`withdrawal_cancellation_cooldown_ms`](../config.mdx#withdrawal_cancellation_cooldown_ms)
  must have elapsed since you submitted the request. The cooldown stops rapid
  submit-and-cancel cycles from interfering with processing.

Common reasons to cancel include a request that is larger than the Guardian
rate limiter's maximum capacity, which Hashi skips until governance raises the limit,
and a destination address you entered incorrectly. See
[Rate Limiting Withdrawals](../limiter.mdx) for how the limiter affects queued
requests.

## Cancel with the CLI

You need the withdrawal request ID that `hashi withdraw request` printed. If
you did not keep it, list your requests:

```bash
hashi withdraw -c hashi-cli.toml list --json
```

Then cancel:

```bash
hashi withdraw -c hashi-cli.toml cancel <request-id>
```

CLI global options such as `-c` belong after the first-level subcommand. See
[Global options](../reference/cli.mdx#global-options).

## Cancel with the TypeScript SDK

Pass the request ID you extracted from the `WithdrawalRequested` event when
you [submitted the withdrawal](withdraw.mdx#withdraw-with-the-typescript-sdk):

```ts
await client.hashi.cancelWithdrawal({ signer, requestId });
```

The SDK does not check the 3 conditions before signing. If any of them fails,
the Sui transaction aborts and your `hBTC` stays locked in the request until
the condition holds or the withdrawal completes.

## After you cancel

Hashi returns the full `hBTC` amount to your Sui address in the same
transaction. The request's status becomes cancelled, and
`client.hashi.view.withdrawalStatus` reports it as `cancelled`. You can
confirm the refund with the balance command or the balance reader described in
[Deposit BTC](deposit.mdx#step-3-check-your-hbtc-balance).

---

## hBTC FAQ

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/hbtc/faq.md

> Answers to common questions about hBTC: backing, timing, minimums, fees, stuck withdrawals, supported addresses, and the HASHI token.

This page answers the questions people ask most often about `hBTC`. Each
answer links to the page that has the full detail.

## What is hBTC, and is it backed 1:1?

`hBTC` is a fungible `Coin<BTC>` on Sui. Hashi mints it when you deposit BTC
and burns it when you withdraw, so every `hBTC` corresponds to BTC held in the
Hashi UTXO pool. The Hashi committee, a subset of Sui validators using threshold
signing, controls the pool together with the Guardian. See
[Introduction](../README.mdx) and [Committee](../committee.mdx).

## Is there a HASHI token?

No. `hBTC` is the only coin Hashi creates. There is no governance, utility, or
airdrop token. Committee members govern the protocol by voting onchain with
their validator stake weight. Treat any HASHI token offering, presale, or
airdrop as an imitation. See [User Flows](../user-flows.mdx).

## Who controls the BTC I deposit?

Every deposit address is a Taproot address that only the Hashi committee and
the Guardian can spend together. No single party holds the key. If the
Guardian key is ever lost, a recovery script lets the committee alone spend a
UTXO 60 days after it confirms, so funds cannot become stranded. See
[Bitcoin Address Scheme](../address-scheme.mdx) and
[Guardian](../guardian.mdx).

## How long does a deposit take?

A deposit passes through 3 waits before Hashi mints `hBTC`:

1. The funding transaction must reach
   [`bitcoin_confirmation_threshold`](../config.mdx#bitcoin_confirmation_threshold)
   Bitcoin blocks, 6 by default, which is about an hour.
2. The committee approves the deposit. On Mainnet, members screen the Bitcoin
   transaction and the Sui recipient first. See
   [Handling Sanctioned Addresses](../sanctions.mdx).
3. After approval, the
   [`bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms`](../config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms)
   window must pass, 10 minutes by default, before anyone can confirm the
   deposit and mint.

A request that is not confirmed within 24 hours expires, and you can submit
the UTXO again. See the [Deposit](../deposit.mdx) lifecycle.

## How long does a withdrawal take?

There is no fixed time. A request waits for committee approval, then for the
leader to batch it with other approved requests, then for capacity in the
Guardian's rate limiter, and finally for the Bitcoin transaction to reach the
confirmation threshold. Most of the variation comes from the rate limiter and
from Bitcoin fee conditions. You can read the limiter's current capacity with
`client.hashi.guardian.canWithdraw` in the SDK before you submit. See
[Rate Limiting Withdrawals](../limiter.mdx) and the [Withdraw](../withdraw.mdx)
lifecycle.

## What are the minimum amounts?

Both minimums are governance parameters, 30,000 satoshis by default:

- [`bitcoin_deposit_minimum`](../config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_minimum) for
  deposits.
- [`bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum`](../config.mdx#bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum)
  for withdrawals. This minimum exists so that every request can pay the
  worst-case miner fee and still leave an output above Bitcoin's dust
  threshold.

Read the live values with `hashi config on-chain` in the CLI or
`client.hashi.view.all()` in the SDK.

## What fees do I pay?

Hashi charges no protocol fee. Deposits are free apart from Sui gas for the
request transaction. Withdrawals pay the Bitcoin miner fee, which Hashi deducts
from your output, plus Sui gas. See [Fees](../fees.mdx).

## Why did I receive less BTC than I withdrew?

The difference is the Bitcoin miner fee for your share of the withdrawal
transaction. Hashi estimates the fee from the connected Bitcoin node, caps it,
and never charges more than the worst-case fee derived from the withdrawal
minimum. See [Withdrawal fees](../fees.mdx#withdrawal-fees).

## Why is my withdrawal still waiting?

Check these causes in order:

- **Rate limiter capacity:** The Guardian's token bucket is empty, and your
  request waits for it to refill. Hashi skips a request larger than the bucket's maximum
  capacity until governance raises the limit. You can
  [cancel it](cancel.mdx).
- **Protocol paused:** When the
  [`paused`](../config.mdx#paused) flag is set, queued requests stay queued
  and resume when the committee unpauses.
- **Reconfiguration:** Hashi pauses withdrawals while the committee hands the
  MPC key to the next epoch's committee. See
  [Reconfiguration](../reconfiguration.mdx).
- **Slow Bitcoin confirmation:** If the transaction is already broadcast, you
  can speed it up by spending your output with a higher-fee child. See
  [Stuck transactions](../fees.mdx#stuck-transactions).

## Which Bitcoin addresses can I withdraw to?

`P2WPKH` (bech32) and `P2TR` (bech32m) addresses on the Bitcoin network that
matches your Sui network. Hashi does not support `P2WSH` or legacy address
types. See [Withdraw BTC](withdraw.mdx#before-you-withdraw).

## Can I deposit the same UTXO twice?

No. Hashi records each UTXO it accepts, and a request for a UTXO that is
already in the pool aborts onchain. In the SDK, check with
`client.hashi.view.findUsedUtxos` before you submit. See
[Deposit BTC](deposit.mdx#deposit-with-the-typescript-sdk).

## I sent BTC but did not record the deposit. Is it lost?

No. The BTC sits at your deposit address until you record it. Hashi mints
`hBTC` only after you submit the deposit request on Sui, so submit it when you
are ready. See [Deposit BTC](deposit.mdx).

## Can Hashi reject a deposit?

Yes, in 3 cases: the amount is below the minimum, the request expires before
the committee confirms it, or a quorum of committee members declines to
approve it after screening. The contract rejects a deposit below the minimum
when you submit the request. See [Handling Sanctioned Addresses](../sanctions.mdx).

## Where can I try Hashi without real BTC?

On Testnet, which pairs Sui Testnet with Bitcoin Signet. Signet coins have no
value and come from public faucets. See
[Try a deposit on Testnet](deposit.mdx#try-a-deposit-on-testnet).

---

## TypeScript SDK

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/ts-sdk.md

> TypeScript SDK for the Hashi protocol. Hashi is a decentralized Bitcoin collateralization primitive on Sui. Orchestrate native BTC directly from smart contracts—without centralized balance sheets.

TypeScript SDK for the [Hashi](https://github.com/MystenLabs/hashi) protocol. Hashi is a
decentralized Bitcoin collateralization primitive on Sui. Orchestrate native BTC directly from smart
contracts—without centralized balance sheets.

:::warning

**Not production-ready.** This SDK is pre-1.0 and under active development. The API may
change without notice and only Sui testnet and devnet are wired up. Do not use it in production
environments yet.

:::

End-user actions only: **deposit**, **request withdrawal**, **cancel withdrawal**.
Operator/committee/relayer calls are intentionally not part of this surface — those tools should
import the generated bindings under `src/contracts/hashi/` directly.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @mysten/hashi @mysten/sui
```

`@mysten/sui` is a peer dependency.

## Setup

The SDK attaches to any Sui client via `$extend`. After extension, every Hashi method lives under
`client.hashi.*`.

```ts

const client = new SuiGrpcClient({
	network: 'testnet',
	baseUrl: 'https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443',
}).$extend(hashi());

const signer = Ed25519Keypair.fromSecretKey(/* … */);
```

> **Network support.** Sui **testnet** and **devnet** are wired up (Bitcoin **signet** by default).
> Prefer testnet — devnet support is temporary and will be deprecated. `hashi()` throws
> on any other network of the client it's extending. To target
> a custom or local deployment, pass `hashiObjectId`, `packageId`, and `bitcoinNetwork` explicitly.

> **Optional client options.** `hashi({ ... })` also accepts `btcRpcUrl` — a Bitcoin Core JSON-RPC
> URL, required for the [`client.hashi.bitcoin.*`](#bitcoin-rpc-optional) lookups — and
> `graphqlUrl`, which overrides the Sui GraphQL endpoint used by
> [`transactionHistory`](#transaction-history) (defaults to
> `https://graphql.{network}.sui.io/graphql`).

## Quickstart: Deposit BTC → mint hBTC

1. Derive the unique P2TR Bitcoin deposit address for your Sui address.
2. Send BTC to that address from any wallet.
3. Submit the funding `txid` + `vout` to Hashi for committee confirmation.

The committee watches the Bitcoin chain. Once the funding tx reaches `bitcoinConfirmationThreshold`
confirmations the committee **approves** the deposit; after an additional
`bitcoinDepositTimeDelayMs` safety window elapses the deposit becomes confirmable and `hBTC` is
minted to the `recipient` address. `view.depositStatus(digest).confirmableAtMs` reports that
earliest mint time.

```ts
const recipient = signer.toSuiAddress();

// 1. Get the deposit address.
const btcAddress = await client.hashi.generateDepositAddress({
	suiAddress: recipient,
});

// 2. Send BTC to `btcAddress` from any wallet, then collect the
//    funding tx's display-order txid and the vout that paid the
//    deposit address. (Display-order = the form mempool.space and
//    `bitcoin-cli` show — the SDK reverses internally.)

// 3. Record the deposit on Sui.
const result = await client.hashi.deposit({
	signer,
	txid: '0x<64-hex display-order txid>',
	utxos: [{ vout: 0, amountSats: 100_000n }],
	recipient,
});

if (result.$kind !== 'Transaction') {
	throw new Error(`deposit failed: ${JSON.stringify(result.FailedTransaction)}`);
}
// `hBTC` lands in `recipient`'s balance once the committee confirms.
```

A single funding tx may pay the deposit address on multiple outputs — pass them all in `utxos` and
they're batched into one atomic Sui PTB.

## Quickstart: Request withdrawal (burn hBTC → receive BTC)

Burns `amountSats` of `hBTC` from the signer's balance and enqueues a request for the committee to
send BTC to `bitcoinAddress`. The address is decoded client-side as bech32 (P2WPKH) or bech32m
(P2TR) and must match the client's configured Bitcoin network.

```ts
const result = await client.hashi.requestWithdrawal({
	signer,
	amountSats: 50_000n,
	bitcoinAddress: 'tb1q…', // P2WPKH on signet/testnet, or `tb1p…` for P2TR
});

if (result.$kind !== 'Transaction') {
	throw new Error(`request failed: ${JSON.stringify(result.FailedTransaction)}`);
}

// Pull the request id out of the WithdrawalRequested — needed if
// you later want to cancel.
const evt = result.Transaction.events?.find((e) =>
	e.eventType.endsWith('::withdrawal_queue::WithdrawalRequested'),
);
const requestId = (evt as { json?: { request_id?: string } } | undefined)?.json?.request_id;
```

## Quickstart: Cancel a pending withdrawal

Returns the locked `hBTC` to the signer. Only the original requester can cancel, only while the
request is still `Requested` or `Approved` (not after committee commitment), and only after
`withdrawalCancellationCooldownMs` has elapsed since the request. All three are enforced on-chain.

```ts
await client.hashi.cancelWithdrawal({ signer, requestId });
```

## Tracking a deposit or withdrawal

`deposit` and `requestWithdrawal` resolve to a transaction execution result whose
`Transaction.digest` identifies the submitted Sui tx. Pass that digest to the `view.*Status` readers
for a one-shot check, or to the `waitFor*` helpers to poll until a terminal state.

```ts
const digest = result.Transaction?.digest;

// One-shot status check — returns null if the digest has no Hashi event.
const deposit = await client.hashi.view.depositStatus(digest);
// deposit?.status: "pending" | "confirmed" | "expired" | "unknown"
// deposit?.approvalTimestampMs — when the committee approved (null until approved)
// deposit?.confirmableAtMs — earliest mint time = approval + bitcoinDepositTimeDelayMs
//                            (null until approved)

const withdrawal = await client.hashi.view.withdrawalStatus(digest);
// withdrawal?.status: "Requested" | "Approved" | "Processing"
//                     | "Signed" | "Confirmed" | "cancelled"
```

To block until the committee finishes, use the polling helpers. They resolve on a terminal state —
deposits on `confirmed`/`expired`, withdrawals on `Confirmed`/`cancelled`:

```ts
const info = await client.hashi.waitForDeposit(digest, {
	intervalMs: 15_000, // default
	signal: AbortSignal.timeout(600_000), // optional cancellation
});

const wInfo = await client.hashi.waitForWithdrawal(digest);
// wInfo.btcTxid is populated once the committee commits the Bitcoin tx.
```

## Checking hBTC balance

```ts
const { totalBalance, coinObjectCount } = await client.hashi.view.balance(signer.toSuiAddress());
// totalBalance — hBTC in satoshis; coinObjectCount — number of coin objects held.
```

## Transaction history

`view.transactionHistory` returns a unified, newest-first list of deposits and withdrawals for a Sui
address. Each item is a discriminated union — switch on `kind`:

```ts
const history = await client.hashi.view.transactionHistory(signer.toSuiAddress());

for (const item of history) {
	if (item.kind === 'deposit') {
		console.log(item.btcTxid, item.amountSats, item.approved);
	} else {
		console.log(item.requestId, item.btcAmountSats, item.status);
	}
}
```

Confirmed requests come from the on-chain index; in-flight deposits are discovered via the Sui
GraphQL endpoint (`graphqlUrl`). If GraphQL is unavailable the call still returns the confirmed set.

## Detecting already-used UTXOs

Before submitting a deposit, check whether its outputs were already recorded — re-submitting a
consumed UTXO aborts on-chain.

```ts
const results = await client.hashi.view.findUsedUtxos([
	{ txid: '0x<64-hex display-order txid>', vout: 0 },
]);
// results[0]: { utxoId, inActivePool, inSpentPool, isUsed }
```

## Estimating fees

```ts
// Withdrawal: worst-case BTC network fee + on-chain minimum. Pass a sender
// to also get a dry-run gas estimate.
const fees = await client.hashi.view.withdrawalFees(signer.toSuiAddress());
// { worstCaseNetworkFeeSats, withdrawalMinimumSats, gasEstimateMist }

// Deposit: dry-run gas estimate only.
const { gasEstimateMist } = await client.hashi.view.depositGasEstimate(signer.toSuiAddress());
```

Gas estimation is best-effort — a failed simulation yields `0n` rather than throwing.

## Reading governance state

Governance parameters — the pause flag, deposit/withdrawal minimums, confirmation threshold, deposit
time delay, and cancellation cooldown — are read through `client.hashi.view`, the same namespace as
the balance, status, history, and fee readers above. Prefer `view.all()` when you need 2+ values —
single round-trip, internally consistent snapshot.

```ts
const snap = await client.hashi.view.all();
// { paused, bitcoinDepositMinimum, bitcoinWithdrawalMinimum,
//   bitcoinConfirmationThreshold, bitcoinDepositTimeDelayMs,
//   withdrawalCancellationCooldownMs, worstCaseNetworkFee, ... }
```

## Errors

Direct methods throw typed errors before signing whenever a precondition can be checked client-side.
`instanceof` to distinguish:

| Error                        | Thrown when                                                                                                |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `InvalidParamsError`         | `txid`/`recipient` not 0x-prefixed 32-byte hex, or `utxos` empty/duplicate                                 |
| `InvalidBitcoinAddressError` | `bitcoinAddress` fails bech32(m) decode or HRP mismatches the BTC network                                  |
| `HashiPausedError`           | Governance has paused the operation (`deposit` or `withdraw`)                                              |
| `AmountBelowMinimumError`    | A UTXO or withdrawal amount is below the on-chain minimum                                                  |
| `HashiFetchError`            | The Hashi shared object can't be read or has an unexpected shape                                           |
| `HashiConfigError`           | A governance config entry is missing or malformed                                                          |
| `HashiGuardianError`         | The guardian `/info` can't be resolved, reached, or parsed, or the limiter isn't initialized (see `.code`) |

## Advanced: composable transactions

The direct methods (`deposit`, `requestWithdrawal`, `cancelWithdrawal`) sign and execute in one
call. For sponsored transactions, dry-runs, or bundling Hashi calls into a larger PTB, use the
`tx.*` builders — they return an unsigned `Transaction` and leave signing to the caller.

```ts
const tx = client.hashi.tx.deposit({ txid, utxos, recipient });
// …add more commands to `tx`, then sign and execute via your usual path.
```

Move-call thunks are also available under `client.hashi.call.*` for direct composition into
hand-built PTBs.

## Bitcoin RPC (optional)

When the client is constructed with a `btcRpcUrl`, the `client.hashi.bitcoin.*` namespace reads the
Bitcoin chain directly — useful for finding which output of a funding tx paid your deposit address,
and for checking confirmations before submitting a deposit.

```ts
const client = new SuiGrpcClient({
	network: 'testnet',
	baseUrl: 'https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443',
}).$extend(hashi({ btcRpcUrl: 'http://user:pass@127.0.0.1:8332' }));

// Which output(s) of the funding tx paid the deposit address?
const output = await client.hashi.bitcoin.lookupVout(btcTxid, btcAddress);
const outputs = await client.hashi.bitcoin.lookupAllVouts(btcTxid, btcAddress);
// each result: { vout, amountSats }

// Confirmation count — 0 while the tx is still in the mempool.
const confirmations = await client.hashi.bitcoin.confirmations(btcTxid);
```

Calling any `bitcoin.*` method without `btcRpcUrl` configured throws.

## Guardian rate limiter (optional)

Withdrawals are co-signed by the Hashi **guardian**, which throttles signing with a token-bucket
rate limiter. When the client can resolve a guardian URL — from `guardianUrl`, a custom
`guardianInfoProvider`, or the on-chain `guardian_url` config — the `client.hashi.guardian.*`
namespace reads the guardian's public, read-only `/info` endpoint to surface that limiter's
headroom.

```ts
// Guardian identity + limiter. `limiter` is null before the guardian is provisioned.
const info = await client.hashi.guardian.info();

// Projected capacity now, bucket fill %, and the refill-to-full ETA.
const status = await client.hashi.guardian.limiterStatus();
// { availableNowSats, bucketFillPercent, fullAtSecs, state, config }

// Can the guardian sign a 50,000-sat withdrawal right now?
const check = await client.hashi.guardian.canWithdraw(50_000n);
// { allowed, availableNowSats, estimatedWaitSecs }
```

`guardianUrl` overrides the on-chain `guardian_url`; a `guardianInfoProvider` overrides both (useful
for caching or a custom transport). The on-chain `guardian_url` is only published at launch, so a
client constructed beforehand re-reads the chain on each call until it resolves — throwing
